title: Parallel Hardware
summary: How modern hardware does many things at once: Flynn's taxonomy and the Amdahl and Gustafson limits, multicore memory consistency models (x86-TSO versus ARM), SIMD vectorisation with SSE, AVX and NEON, GPU architecture with warps and SIMT, accelerators such as TPUs and FPGAs, and how to measure performance with perf and the roofline model.

lessons.title: Flynn's taxonomy, Amdahl and Gustafson
lessons.summary: The four classic ways hardware can be parallel, and the two laws that tell you how much faster more cores can actually make a program.
lessons.body:
Clock scaling and microarchitectural improvements contributed to single-thread performance growth. Power and thermal constraints made rapid clock increases harder in the mid-2000s; clock rates and single-core performance did not stop improving. Designers also pursued more cores, vector execution and specialised accelerators.

Parallel hardware only helps if the work can be split. This lesson gives you two tools. **Flynn's taxonomy** is a vocabulary for *how* hardware is parallel. **Amdahl's law** and **Gustafson's law** tell you *how much* that parallelism can buy.

## Flynn's taxonomy

Flynn’s taxonomy classifies computers by two questions. How many **instruction streams** run at once? And how many **data streams** does each one act on?

| Class | Instr. | Data | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| SISD | 1 | 1 | Classic single core |
| SIMD | 1 | Many | AVX, NEON, vector units |
| MISD | Many | 1 | Abstract multiple-instruction/single-data class |
| MIMD | Many | Many | Multicore CPUs, clusters |

```
SISD             SIMD
 I -> [PU] <- D   I -> [PU] <- D0
                     -> [PU] <- D1
                     -> [PU] <- D2
MIMD
 I0 -> [PU] <- D0
 I1 -> [PU] <- D1
 I2 -> [PU] <- D2
```

- **SISD** (single instruction, single data): one instruction operates on one piece of data at a time. This is the mental model of a simple CPU, even though real cores pipeline and overlap work internally.
- **SIMD** (single instruction, multiple data): one instruction applies the same operation to many data elements. The 256-bit YMM form of AVX `vaddps` adds eight pairs of float32 values; narrower and wider forms differ.
- **MISD** (multiple instruction, single data): several different operations on the same data. Its classification depends on the instruction and data streams being modelled. Redundant voting systems are not automatically MISD: identical replicated instruction streams do not establish multiple different instruction streams.
- **MIMD** (multiple instruction, multiple data): processors with independent instruction streams operating on multiple data streams. They may execute the same program and share data; ordinary multicore CPUs can provide MIMD execution.

### Modern refinements

Flynn's four boxes are coarse. Real machines mix them, and some extra terms are common:

- **SPMD** (single program, multiple data) is a *programming* style in which participants run the same program on different data, potentially taking different branches. It can be used on MIMD CPUs or SIMT GPUs; MPI also supports other programming styles.
- **SIMT** (single instruction, multiple threads) is NVIDIA's term for GPUs. You write scalar code for one thread; the hardware groups 32 threads into a **GPU warp** and issues instructions to active threads within it. Divergence and independent thread scheduling mean software must never assume implicit lockstep synchronisation. Lesson 4 covers it.
- A CPU can combine MIMD across cores with SIMD within cores. A hypothetical 16-core design sustaining one 512-bit float32 add per core per cycle would produce 16 cores × 16 lanes = 256 additions per cycle. ISA width alone does not specify instruction throughput.

## Speedup and efficiency

Before the laws, two definitions. Both compare the time the same job takes on one processor with the time it takes on several. **Speedup** says how many times faster the parallel run is; **parallel efficiency** says how much of that speedup each processor contributes.

```formula
S(n) = T(1) / T(n)
E(n) = S(n) / n
where
S(n): the speedup on n processors: how many times faster the n-processor run finishes than the one-processor run (a plain ratio, no unit)
T(1): the run time of the job on one processor, in seconds (s)
T(n): the run time of the same job on n processors, in seconds (s)
n: the number of processors (for example CPU cores) used
E(n): the parallel efficiency on n processors: speedup per processor, normally between 0 and 1 (often given as a percentage)
In words: speedup is old time divided by new time, and efficiency divides that speedup by the number of processors you paid for.
```

For example, a job that takes 100 s on one core and 20 s on 8 cores has a speedup of 100 / 20 = 5× and an efficiency of 5 / 8 = 0.625, or 62.5%.

**Linear speedup** means the speedup equals the number of processors, so efficiency is 1 (100%). Efficiency may fall as processors are added because of serial work, communication, load imbalance or shared resources. It need not decrease monotonically.

## Amdahl's law: the serial part wins

Gene Amdahl's 1967 argument is simple. Split a program's single-core run time into a **parallel fraction** that can be spread across processors and a **serial fraction** that cannot (start-up, reading input, a final merge, anything inherently sequential). For a fixed amount of work, assume equally fast processors, unchanged serial time, perfect division of the parallel work and no new overhead. Then only the parallel part shrinks, and dividing the old time by the new time gives the speedup:

```formula
T(n) = T(1) × ((1 − p) + p / n)
S(n) = T(1) / T(n)
S(n) = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / n)
where
T(n): the run time on n processors, in seconds (s)
T(1): the run time on one processor, in seconds (s)
p: the parallel fraction: the share of the one-processor run time that can be split across processors, from 0 to 1 (0.9 means 90%)
1 − p: the serial fraction, the share that cannot be split and keeps its full length
n: the number of processors
S(n): the speedup on n processors, a plain ratio
In words: the serial part keeps its full length while the parallel part is divided by the number of processors, and the speedup is one over the new, shorter, total.
```

Add processors and the parallel term p / n shrinks to almost nothing, but the serial term never does. That sets a ceiling:

```formula
S_max = 1 / (1 − p)
S_max = 1 / (1 − 0.9) = 1 / 0.1 = 10
where
S_max: the highest speedup reachable: the value S(n) approaches as the number of processors n grows without limit
S(n): Amdahl's speedup on n processors
p: the parallel fraction of the one-processor run time, from 0 to 1; here 0.9
n: the number of processors
In words: however many processors you add, the speedup can never beat one over the serial fraction; with 10% serial work the limit is 10×.
```

The ceiling exists only while some work is serial. If all of it were parallel (p = 1), this ideal model would give a speedup equal to n, with no finite ceiling. Here is the same formula as code:

```python
def amdahl(p, n):
    if not 0 <= p <= 1:
        raise ValueError("p outside [0, 1]")
    if type(n) is not int or n < 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid n")
    return 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)

for n in [2, 8, 64, 1024]:
    print(n, round(amdahl(0.9, n), 2))
# 2 1.82
# 8 4.71
# 64 8.77
# 1024 9.91
```

With 90% of the work parallel, the ceiling is 10×. Going from 64 to 1,024 cores, sixteen times the hardware, takes you from 8.8× to 9.9×.

**Example: where the time goes.** Take a job that is 90% parallel and takes 100 s on one core, and run it on 8 cores:

```formula
T(8) = 100 s × ((1 − 0.9) + 0.9 / 8)
T(8) = 10 s + 11.25 s = 21.25 s
S(8) = 100 s / 21.25 s ≈ 4.7
E(8) = 4.7 / 8 ≈ 0.59
where
T(8): the run time on 8 cores, in seconds (s)
S(8): the speedup on 8 cores, a plain ratio
E(8): the parallel efficiency on 8 cores (0.59 means 59%)
s: second, the unit of time
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
In words: the 10 s serial part stays 10 s, the 90 s parallel part drops to 11.25 s, so the job runs about 4.7 times faster and each core is used about 59% effectively.
```

The 10 s serial part is now nearly half the run.

As the parallel portion shrinks, the serial portion can become more important. Profile again and compare achievable total-time reductions, including new overhead and implementation cost.

### Amdahl beyond cores

The law applies to any optimisation that speeds up only part of the work, not just to adding cores. Replace "divided across n processors" with "made k times faster":

```formula
S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f / k)
S = 1 / ((1 − 0.6) + 0.6 / 20)
S = 1 / (0.4 + 0.03) = 1 / 0.43 ≈ 2.3
where
S: the overall speedup of the whole job, a plain ratio
f: the fraction of the original run time that the change speeds up, from 0 to 1; here 0.6
k: how many times faster that part becomes (its local speedup); here 20
≈: approximately equal to
In words: if a GPU makes 60% of a job 20 times faster, the untouched 40% still dominates, and the whole job is only about 2.3 times faster.
```

The actual benefit must also cover transfer and setup costs; even a smaller offloaded fraction can be worthwhile if its saving justifies those costs.

## Gustafson's law: grow the problem

Amdahl assumes a **fixed problem size** (strong scaling). In 1988 John Gustafson, working on a 1,024-processor machine at Sandia, described workloads that use larger machines to solve **bigger problems** in approximately the same time: finer weather grids, larger simulations, more training data.

Gustafson measures fractions on the *parallel* run instead: the **serial fraction of the parallel run**. Assume the serial duration is unchanged, all processors have equal speed and the measured parallel interval contains perfectly divided useful work rather than added overhead. Now ask how long one processor would need for that same, larger job. The serial part takes the same time, but the parallel part, which kept n processors busy, would take n times as long:

```formula
T(n) = s + (1 − s) = 1
T(1) = s + (1 − s) × n
S(n) = T(1) / T(n) = s + (1 − s) × n
S(n) = n − s × (n − 1)
where
T(n): the run time on n processors, used as the unit of time (so it equals 1)
T(1): the time one processor would need for the same scaled job, in units of the n-processor run time
s: the serial fraction measured on the n-processor run, from 0 to 1
1 − s: the parallel fraction of the n-processor run
n: the number of processors
S(n): the scaled speedup on n processors, a plain ratio
In words: one processor would need the serial time plus n copies of the parallel time, so the speedup grows in a straight line with the number of processors, minus a small loss for the serial part.
```

This is the **scaled speedup**. It is linear in n when the parallel-run serial fraction s is held fixed. For example, with 10% serial time on 64 processors:

```formula
S(64) = 0.1 + (1 − 0.1) × 64
S(64) = 0.1 + 57.6 = 57.7
where
S(64): the scaled speedup on 64 processors, a plain ratio
0.1: the serial fraction measured on the 64-processor run
In words: a job that is 10% serial on 64 processors would take about 57.7 times as long on one processor.
```

### Are they contradictory?

No. They answer different questions.

| | Amdahl | Gustafson |
|---|---|---|
| Problem size | Fixed | Grows with processor count |
| Scaling view | Strong scaling | Scaled work; related to weak scaling |
| Fraction measured on | 1-core run | Parallel run |
| Model result | Ceiling unless all work is parallel | Linear for a fixed serial fraction |

The key is that in many real problems the serial work (reading a config, setting up) stays roughly constant while the parallel work grows with the data. So the *serial fraction shrinks* as the problem grows. For example, if serial work stays fixed and parallel work grows 1,000-fold, an original 10% serial fraction becomes:

```formula
f_s = t_s / (t_s + t_p)
f_s = 0.1 / (0.1 + 0.9 × 1,000)
f_s = 0.1 / 900.1 ≈ 0.000111
where
f_s: the serial fraction of the one-processor work after the problem has grown (0.000111 is 0.0111%)
t_s: the serial work, unchanged at 0.1 of the original one-processor run time
t_p: the parallel work: 0.9 of the original run, grown 1,000-fold
≈: approximately equal to
In words: when only the parallel work grows, the fixed serial part becomes a tiny share of the total, here about one ten-thousandth.
```

- If your goal is **latency** (render this one frame faster), Amdahl rules. Think of a web request or a compile.
- If your goal is **throughput or capability** (simulate a bigger system in an hour), Gustafson is the better model. Think of HPC and ML training.

## Why real speedups differ from the models

Both laws are optimistic. They assume the parallel part splits perfectly. Real code also pays for:

- **Communication and synchronisation.** Locks, barriers and message passing add time that often *grows* with n.
- **Load imbalance.** The slowest worker decides when the whole job finishes.
- **Shared resources.** Cores share memory bandwidth and the last-level cache. A loop may stop scaling once the memory bandwidth on offer is saturated; the core count depends on the machine, access pattern and memory placement.
- **Coherence traffic.** Cores writing to the same cache line, even different variables in it (false sharing), bounce the line between caches.

A useful diagnostic is the **Karp–Flatt metric**, the experimentally determined serial fraction. It runs Amdahl's law backwards: take a measured speedup and ask what serial fraction would have produced it. Writing Amdahl's law with the serial fraction e (so the parallel fraction is 1 − e) and solving for e gives:

```formula
1 / S = e + (1 − e) / n
e = (1/S − 1/n) / (1 − 1/n)
where
e: the Karp–Flatt metric: the serial fraction that would make Amdahl's law reproduce the measured speedup, normally between 0 and 1
S: the speedup you measured on n processors, a plain ratio
n: the number of processors, more than 1
In words: the metric is the serial fraction implied by a measured speedup; a value that stays constant as you add processors fits Amdahl's model, and one that rises means something else is costing time.
```

For example, a 6× speedup on 8 processors gives:

```formula
e = (1/6 − 1/8) / (1 − 1/8)
e = 0.0417 / 0.875 ≈ 0.048
where
e: the Karp–Flatt metric (0.048 means the program behaves as if about 4.8% of it were serial)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a 6× speedup on 8 processors is what Amdahl's law predicts for a program that is about 4.8% serial.
```

For comparable fixed-work measurements, compute e at several processor counts. A constant value is consistent with an Amdahl-style limit, not proof of its cause. Rising e motivates checking added overhead, imbalance, bandwidth, frequency changes and measurement conditions. If S > n, e is negative and is not a literal fraction of serial source code.

> [!warning] Superlinear speedup
> Occasionally the speedup is larger than the number of processors. One possible cause is improved cache residency when data is divided among cores. Other causes include changed algorithmic work or baseline differences. If cache residency is the cause, growing each partition beyond cache capacity may reduce that benefit; disappearance is not guaranteed from speedup alone.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> A hardware-specific saturation-core count and a definitive catalogue of MISD products is omitted because comparable measurements and a consistent stream-level classification were not reliably established here.

## Key takeaways
- Flynn classifies instruction and data streams as SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD. Machines can combine models at different levels.
- Amdahl: for a fixed problem, the serial fraction caps speedup at one divided by that fraction, however many processors you add. With 5% fixed serial time, that model’s limit is 20×.
- Gustafson: under ideal work-scaling assumptions, scaled speedup grows linearly with the number of processors when the parallel run's serial fraction is fixed.
- Amdahl measures fractions on the one-core run, Gustafson on the n-core run. Fixed work versus scaled work; the latter is related to weak scaling.
- Real speedups also lose to communication, imbalance and shared bandwidth. A rising Karp–Flatt metric motivates investigating changing overhead or execution conditions.

questions.prompt: Profiling shows that 95% of a program's single-core run time is perfectly parallelisable and 5% is strictly serial. According to Amdahl's law, what is the maximum speedup you could ever get, however many cores you add? Assume equal per-core speed, fixed work, unchanged serial time and no added overhead.

options.explanation: This confuses the parallel percentage with a speedup. The serial 5% never shrinks, so the bound comes from it.
Correct. The ceiling is 1 / (1 − 0.95) = 1 / 0.05 = 20. Even infinitely many cores leave the 5% serial part untouched.

options.text: Unlimited, given enough cores
options.explanation: That is Gustafson's scaled view for a growing problem. For a fixed problem, the serial part caps speedup.
This inverts the fraction incorrectly. 5% serial means the serial part is one twentieth of the time, giving a cap of 20×, not 5×.

questions.workedExample:
Amdahl's law gives the speedup on n cores. As n grows without limit, the parallel term shrinks to almost nothing and only the serial term is left:

```formula
S(n) = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / n)
S_max = 1 / (1 − p)
S_max = 1 / (1 − 0.95) = 1 / 0.05 = 20
where
S(n): the speedup on n cores, a plain ratio
p: the parallel fraction of the single-core run time; 0.95 here
n: the number of cores
S_max: the ceiling: the value S(n) approaches as n grows without limit
In words: with 5% serial work, no number of cores can make the program more than 20 times faster.
```

Intuition: with a 100 s run, 5 s is serial. Even if the other 95 s drops to zero, you still wait 5 s, and 100 / 5 = 20.

options.text: MIMD: several independent instruction streams, each on its own data
options.explanation: Correct. Each core fetches its own instructions and works on its own data, which is the definition of MIMD.

options.text: SIMD: all cores execute the same instruction
options.explanation: The cores are running entirely different programs, so they are not in lockstep on one instruction stream.

options.text: SISD, because each core is a single processor
options.explanation: Each core alone is SISD-like, but the chip as a whole runs multiple instruction streams at once.

options.text: MISD: multiple programs share the same data
options.explanation: The browser, compiler and music player work on different data, and MISD is a rarely used class.

questions.workedExample:
Count the streams across the whole chip:

- Instruction streams: three different programs, so many.
- Data streams: each program has its own data, so many.

Many and many is **MIMD**. The described independently executing cores provide MIMD execution. Inside each core, vector instructions may additionally be SIMD.

options.explanation: This multiplies 0.8 by 4. Speedup is the ratio of times, and the serial 20% still takes its full time.

Work in time units. Say the single-core run takes 100 s: 20 s serial and 80 s parallel.

```formula
T(4) = 20 s + 80 s / 4 = 40 s
S(4) = 100 s / 40 s = 2.5
E(4) = 2.5 / 4 = 0.625
where
T(4): the run time on 4 cores, in seconds (s)
S(4): the speedup on 4 cores, a plain ratio
E(4): the parallel efficiency on 4 cores (0.625 is 62.5%)

In words: the serial 20 s stays, the parallel 80 s shrinks to 20 s, so 100 s becomes 40 s, a 2.5× speedup.
```

questions.prompt: Which statements about Amdahl's and Gustafson's laws are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Amdahl's law assumes the total problem size stays fixed as processors are added
options.explanation: Correct. Amdahl models strong scaling: the same job on more processors.

options.text: Gustafson's law assumes the problem grows so that run time stays roughly constant
options.explanation: Correct. Gustafson considers scaled workloads, often at fixed run time. This is related to weak scaling; exact weak-scaling experiments also specify how work per processor is held constant.

options.text: The two laws contradict each other, so at most one can be right
options.explanation: They answer different questions (fixed versus scaled workload) and measure the serial fraction on different runs. Both are correct for their assumptions.

options.text: Gustafson's law shows that serial code no longer matters at all
options.explanation: The serial fraction is still in the formula. It matters less only because, in many problems, serial work stays constant while parallel work grows.

options.text: For speeding up a single interactive request, Amdahl's model is usually the relevant one
options.explanation: Correct. A single request has fixed work; you want it to finish sooner, which is strong scaling.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each claim:

1. Amdahl: fixed workload, more processors. **True.**
2. Gustafson: workload scales with n. **True.**
3. Contradiction? No. Amdahl's p is a fraction of the one-core run; Gustafson's s is a fraction of the n-core run.
4. Serial code still costs s in the formula. **False.**
5. One request has a fixed amount of work: latency, strong scaling, Amdahl. **True.**

questions.workedExample:
Amdahl's law applies to any change that speeds up only part of a job:

```formula
S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f / k)
S_A = 1 / (0.7 + 0.3 / 10) = 1 / 0.73
S_A ≈ 1.37
S_B = 1 / (0.3 + 0.7 / 2) = 1 / 0.65
S_B ≈ 1.54
where
S: the overall speedup of the whole job
f: the fraction of the original time that is improved: 0.3 for the disk (A), 0.7 for the computation (B)
k: how many times faster that part becomes: 10 for A, 2 for B
S_A: the overall speedup from option A
S_B: the overall speedup from option B
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a modest speedup of the big 70% part beats a large speedup of the small 30% part.
```

Even an infinitely fast disk would cap option A at 1 / 0.7 ≈ 1.43×, still below B. Compare attainable whole-job time savings and implementation cost.

Efficiency 75%, serial fraction 25%

questions.workedExample:
Step by step:

```formula
E = S / n = 6 / 8 = 0.75
e = (1/S − 1/n) / (1 − 1/n)
e = (0.1667 − 0.125) / 0.875
e = 0.0417 / 0.875 ≈ 0.048
where
E: the parallel efficiency (0.75 is 75%)
S: the measured speedup; 6
n: the number of cores; 8
e: the Karp–Flatt metric: the serial fraction that would make Amdahl's law give the measured speedup
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a 6× speedup on 8 cores is 75% efficient and behaves as if about 4.8% of the program were serial.
```

Check with Amdahl: 1 / (0.048 + 0.952 / 8) ≈ 1 / 0.167 ≈ 6.0. It matches.

questions.prompt: You measure a parallel sort: 1.9× on 2 cores, 3.4× on 4 cores, 5.0× on 8 cores. The Karp–Flatt serial fraction comes out at about 0.053, 0.059 and 0.086. What does this pattern most likely tell you?

options.text: The program has a fixed serial section, and Amdahl's law fully explains the results
options.explanation: A fixed serial section would give a roughly constant Karp–Flatt value. Here it rises by over 60% from 2 to 8 cores.

options.text: Overheads that grow with core count, such as synchronisation, contention or shared bandwidth, are limiting scaling
options.explanation: Correct. A rising experimentally determined serial fraction is evidence to investigate overhead or other changing conditions; it does not identify one cause by itself.

options.text: The measurements must be wrong, because the serial fraction is a constant property of the code
options.explanation: The Karp–Flatt value is measured, not a fixed property. Rising values are a real and common diagnostic signal.

options.text: The program shows superlinear speedup from cache effects
options.explanation: All speedups are below n (1.9 < 2, 3.4 < 4, 5.0 < 8), so there is nothing superlinear.

questions.workedExample:
Compute the Karp–Flatt metric at each core count:

```formula
e = (1/S − 1/n) / (1 − 1/n)
e_2 = (0.526 − 0.500) / 0.500 ≈ 0.053
e_4 = (0.294 − 0.250) / 0.750 ≈ 0.059
e_8 = (0.200 − 0.125) / 0.875 ≈ 0.086
where
e: the Karp–Flatt metric, the experimentally determined serial fraction
S: the measured speedup: 1.9, 3.4 and 5.0
n: the number of cores: 2, 4 and 8
e_2: the metric on 2 cores
e_4: the metric on 4 cores
e_8: the metric on 8 cores
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the implied serial fraction grows as cores are added, which a fixed serial section cannot explain.
```

Under pure Amdahl, e would be flat. It grows, so the fixed-cost ideal model does not fit. Added overhead is one possible cause; check frequency, workload and measurement comparability too. For a sort, likely culprits are the merge phase's communication, lock contention, and memory bandwidth shared by all cores. Next step: profile on 8 cores and look for time in locks, barriers or stalled memory loads.

questions.prompt: A large float32 array sum scales well to 4 cores then stays flat to 16. Measurements show DRAM throughput already at this machine’s sustainable limit, with little synchronisation overhead. What is the most likely limit?

options.text: Amdahl's law: the loop must have a hidden 25% serial part
options.explanation: A 25% serial part would give a speedup well under 4 at 4 cores (1 / (0.25 + 0.75/4) ≈ 2.3), not good scaling then a flat line.

options.text: False sharing on the loop counter
options.explanation: The supplied measurements point to saturated DRAM bandwidth. False sharing cannot be ruled out merely because a variable is a loop counter or because scaling initially improved.

options.text: Shared memory bandwidth: a few cores already saturate DRAM, so extra cores just wait
options.explanation: Correct under the given measurement. A float32 sum has low useful arithmetic intensity, and extra cores cannot exceed the measured memory-system ceiling without changing traffic or the available bandwidth.

options.text: The OS refuses to schedule more than 4 threads per process
options.explanation: There is no general four-thread-per-process OS rule. Affinity, CPU quotas or placement can limit concurrency, but the prompt supplies bandwidth measurements as the limiting evidence.

questions.workedExample: A float32 sum performs about one addition per 4 useful bytes. Here actual traffic measurements establish saturated DRAM bandwidth. Additional cores share that same ceiling; investigate traffic reduction or memory-system changes. No universal per-core bandwidth or saturation count is implied.

questions.prompt: A physics simulation shows 9.2× speedup on 8 cores. Which statements are reasonable? Select all that apply.

options.text: This is superlinear speedup, since 9.2 > 8
options.explanation: Correct. Speedup above n is, by definition, superlinear.

options.text: One possible cause is that each core's slice of the data now fits in its cache, when the whole data set did not fit in one core's
options.explanation: Possible when the platform supplies useful additional per-core cache capacity and the partitioned working sets fit it. Cache topology and residency must be measured.

options.text: It disproves Amdahl's law
options.explanation: Amdahl assumes the per-unit work costs the same on 1 or n processors. Cache effects change that cost, so the assumption, not the maths, is violated.

options.text: If improved cache residency caused the effect, it may shrink when every partition outgrows the relevant cache
options.explanation: Correct as a conditional possibility. Other causes of superlinear speedup and changing cache behaviour require separate investigation.

options.text: Parallel efficiency is 115%
options.explanation: Correct. Efficiency = 9.2 / 8 = 1.15.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
E = S / n = 9.2 / 8 = 1.15
where
E: the parallel efficiency (1.15 is 115%)
S: the measured speedup; 9.2
n: the number of cores; 8
In words: each core contributes more than a whole core's worth of speedup, which is what superlinear means.
```

Better cache residency is one possible cause, and may weaken if partitions outgrow cache. It does not disprove Amdahl’s algebra: fixed-work cost assumptions may fail. Check baseline quality, equivalent work, results, compiler settings and frequency before interpreting the result.

questions.prompt: You need a 50× speedup on 100 cores for a fixed-size job. According to Amdahl's law, what fraction of the single-core run time must be parallelisable, at minimum? Assume equal per-core speed, fixed work, unchanged serial time and no added overhead.

options.explanation: With a parallel fraction of 0.5 the ceiling is only 2×, whatever the core count.

options.text: About 99%
options.explanation: Correct. Solving Amdahl's formula for a 50× speedup on 100 cores gives a parallel fraction of 0.98 / 0.99 ≈ 0.990.
A parallel fraction of 0.98 gives 1 / (0.02 + 0.0098) ≈ 33.6×. You need slightly more.
That would give about 91×, well beyond what is required.

questions.workedExample:
Set Amdahl's speedup equal to 50 with n = 100 and solve for p:

```formula
S = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / n)
50 = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / 100)
(1 − p) + p / 100 = 1 / 50 = 0.02
1 − 0.99 × p = 0.02
p = 0.98 / 0.99 ≈ 0.9899
where
S: the speedup required; 50
p: the parallel fraction of the single-core run time, from 0 to 1
n: the number of cores; 100
≈: approximately equal to
In words: to reach 50× on 100 cores, about 99% of the single-core time must be parallel, leaving at most about 1% serial.
```

At this scale, reducing fixed serial time can significantly change the bound; assess I/O and setup costs for the actual workload.

lessons.title: Multicore memory consistency models
lessons.summary: Why cores can see each other's writes in surprising orders, how x86-TSO differs from ARM's weaker model, and how fences and acquire/release atomics restore sanity.
lessons.body:
Cache coherence (from the memory hierarchy module) guarantees that all cores agree on the history of writes to *one* address. It says nothing about the order in which a core sees writes to *different* addresses. That second question is the job of the **memory consistency model**, and mistakes can produce intermittent, platform-dependent bugs.

## The model you expect: sequential consistency

Leslie Lamport defined **sequential consistency** (SC) in 1979. A multicore is SC if the result of any run is the same as if all cores' operations were executed in *some single interleaving*, with each core's operations appearing in program order.

Take two threads and two variables, both initially 0. This is the **store buffering** (SB) litmus test:

```
x = y = 0
Thread 1       Thread 2
x = 1          y = 1
r1 = y         r2 = x
```

Under SC, at least one store must come first in the interleaving, so at least one thread must see a 1. The possible outcomes for `(r1, r2)` are `(0, 1)`, `(1, 0)` or `(1, 1)`. **`(0, 0)` is impossible.**

The x86-TSO model permits (0, 0) for the ordinary-memory accesses described below. A particular experiment need not observe every permitted outcome; failure to observe it does not prove SC.

## Why hardware breaks SC

A store may wait for cache-line ownership or other resources. A **store buffer** can decouple execution/retirement from making committed stores globally observable, allowing independent work to continue while capacity remains. Later loads can execute while earlier stores are still waiting in the buffer.

```
 Core 1               Core 2
 [store buf: x=1]     [store buf: y=1]
      |  r1=y reads 0      |  r2=x reads 0
      v                    v
 ======== shared memory: x=0, y=0 ========
```

Both stores are sitting in buffers, invisible to the other core. Both loads read memory and get 0. Each core's own view is consistent (a same-address load in the abstract model reads its newest buffered store; real **store-to-load forwarding** can require matching size/alignment or waiting), but globally the store appears to have happened after the load.

Out-of-order execution, non-blocking caches and compilers can reorder memory operations too. SC constrains observable outcomes, not necessarily speculative internal execution. Speculation, caches and store buffers can coexist with SC if violations are prevented or detected and recovered. Weaker models allow additional observable behaviours.

## x86-TSO: only one relaxation

x86 implements **total store order** (TSO), formalised by Sewell, Owens and colleagues as x86-TSO. Here the model covers aligned, same-size ordinary loads/stores in coherent write-back memory, excluding non-temporal accesses, MMIO, mixed-size overlap and self-modifying code. It is essentially "SC plus a FIFO store buffer per hardware thread":

- Stores leave each core's buffer **in program order** and enter a single global order visible to other threads. This is an abstract ordering guarantee, not zero propagation delay or wall-clock simultaneity.
- A load can complete while older stores to *other* addresses are still buffered. So **store → load** reordering is visible.
- Loads are not reordered with older loads; stores are not reordered with older loads or older stores.

| Reordering | x86-TSO | ARMv8 |
|---|---|---|
| Load → load | No | Yes |
| Load → store | No | Yes |
| Store → store | No | Yes |
| Store → load | **Yes** | Yes |

To forbid store → load reordering on x86, insert `MFENCE` (drain the store buffer before later loads) or use any `LOCK`-prefixed instruction such as `lock xadd`, or `xchg` with memory, which is implicitly locked. All of these act as full barriers.

## ARM: weakly ordered

For ordinary Normal-memory accesses to independent addresses, the AArch64 model permits all four broad reorderings unless a dependency, barrier or ordered instruction constrains them. These labels summarise observable behaviour rather than a physical implementation. The hardware is free to let a later load overtake an earlier one, or to drain stores to memory out of order.

What forces order on ARM:

- **Dependencies.** An actual machine-level address dependency can order the dependent access. A C/C++ source expression such as `p = head; v = p->val` does not by itself establish a safe inter-thread publication protocol; use appropriate atomics and lifetime rules.
- **Barriers.** For the relevant observers in the inner-shareable domain, `DMB ISH` orders the required earlier and later data accesses; it is not an instruction barrier or a general cache flush. `DMB ISHST` orders stores with stores; `DMB ISHLD` orders loads with later loads and stores.
- **Acquire and release instructions.** `LDAR` (load-acquire) prevents later accesses moving before it. `STLR` (store-release) prevents earlier accesses moving after it. FEAT_LRCPC provides `LDAPR`, an RCpc acquire with weaker ordering in some patterns than `LDAR`; instruction availability and performance depend on the target.

The classic victim is the **message-passing litmus test** (MP):

```
data = flag = 0
Thread 1         Thread 2
data = 42        r1 = flag
flag = 1         r2 = data
```

Can Thread 2 end with `r1 == 1` and `r2 == 0`, that is, the flag set but the data stale? On x86, no: stores leave in order, and loads are not reordered with loads. On ARM, yes: either the two stores or the two loads may be reordered. These are machine-level litmus tests. Using unsynchronised ordinary shared C/C++ objects would already be a data race and undefined behaviour on either target.

### Multi-copy atomicity

A subtler property is **other-multi-copy atomicity**: after a write becomes observable to another observer, the model requires a consistent propagation order to the remaining observers, while the issuing thread may read its own buffered write early. This is not a zero-latency physical event. The revised Armv8-A model described by Pulte et al. and x86-TSO have this property.

For the **IRIW** test, two writers independently update x and y, while two readers read them in opposite orders. If each reader’s loads are suitably ordered at the hardware level, a multicopy-atomic model forbids the readers from observing opposite write orders. A non-multicopy-atomic model can allow it. Language-level acquire operations and different hardware barriers are not interchangeable; specify the actual mapping when comparing architectures.

## Language memory models

You rarely write fences in assembly. C11/C++11, Java, Rust and Go define their own memory model, and the compiler emits whatever each CPU needs. The C/C++ model has two big rules:

1. A **data race** (potentially concurrent conflicting actions, at least one non-atomic, with neither happening before the other) is undefined behaviour.
2. **DRF-SC:** programs that use mutexes and seq_cst operations to prevent data races, and no other weaker synchronisation operations, behave as if sequentially consistent.

Weaker orderings trade simplicity for speed:

| Order | Guarantee |
|---|---|
| `relaxed` | Atomicity and per-object coherence; no publication of unrelated data |
| `release` (store) | Earlier accesses stay before it |
| `acquire` (load) | Later accesses stay after it |
| `seq_cst` | Appropriate acquire/release effects plus one order of seq_cst operations |

Here is one-shot message passing in C11. Assume exactly one producer call and one consumer call, objects initialised before the threads start, and no later concurrent modification or reuse of data. The snippet supplies the thread bodies, not thread creation. The release store "publishes" everything written before it; an acquire load that reads the published value "sees" all of it.

```c
#include <stdatomic.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int data;          /* plain variable */
atomic_int ready;  /* the flag */

void producer(void) {
  data = 42;
  atomic_store_explicit(&ready, 1,
      memory_order_release);
}

void consumer(void) {
  while (!atomic_load_explicit(&ready,
             memory_order_acquire))
    ;  /* spin */
  printf("%d\n", data);  /* always 42 */
}
```

Illustrative compiler mappings for naturally aligned, lock-free 32-bit atomics on ordinary memory (compiler, target features and whether the result is used can change them):

| C11 operation | x86-64 | ARMv8 |
|---|---|---|
| load acquire | `mov` | `ldar` / `ldapr` |
| store release | `mov` | `stlr` |
| store seq_cst | `xchg` | `stlr` |
| seq_cst fetch_add, result used | `lock xadd` | `ldaddal` with LSE, or exclusive loop |

For such x86 loads/stores, acquire/release may need no extra hardware instruction beyond MOV, but still constrain compiler transformations and still incur ordinary memory-access costs. A common seq_cst-store mapping uses memory XCHG or MOV followed by MFENCE. AArch64 mappings using STLR followed by LDAR provide stronger ordering than the minimum language release/acquire requirement; this does not make all atomics cheap. LSE atomics require target support; other mappings use exclusive-load/store loops or library helpers.

> [!warning] Acquire/release does not by itself forbid store buffering
> At the C/C++ language level, both acquire loads in SB may read the initial zeros, so neither reads from the other thread’s release store. There is no synchronises-with edge connecting the threads, and (0, 0) remains permitted. A particular target mapping may be stronger and forbid it. Making all four operations seq_cst is one sufficient solution; correctly placed seq_cst fences or a suitable lock protocol are alternatives. A hardware fence alone does not repair a C/C++ data race on ordinary objects.

## Pitfalls

- **`volatile` is not a synchronisation tool in C or C++.** Volatile accesses obey their language-specific observable-access rules, but do not supply C/C++ inter-thread atomicity or synchronisation. Java volatile has different synchronisation semantics; that does not make an arbitrary racy Java program sequentially consistent.
- **The compiler reorders too.** Even on x86, plain `data = 42; flag = 1;` may be swapped by the optimiser. A correctly designed atomic protocol constrains both compiler and hardware behaviour; merely changing a variable to atomic does not fix every protocol.
- **"Works on my machine."** Testing on x86 cannot find bugs that only weak ordering exposes. Run concurrency tests on ARM, and use ThreadSanitizer to catch data races.
- **Relaxed is for counters.** An atomic fetch_add with relaxed ordering can accumulate an independent statistic without lost increments; separate load-plus-store is not an atomic increment. Publishing unrelated data through a flag needs additional synchronisation.
- **seq_cst by default.** Use the default ordering unless profiling shows the barrier matters. Measure any claimed performance benefit before weakening a proven protocol.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Rosetta performance attribution and a version-independent Linux spinlock instruction catalogue is omitted because the exact implementation contracts and representative measurements were not reliably established; model-level ordering is taught instead.

## Key takeaways
- Coherence orders writes to one address; the consistency model orders accesses to different addresses.
- SC is an observable ordering model. Letting a later load bypass an earlier buffered store can produce non-SC outcomes.
- x86-TSO allows only store → load reordering, so the store-buffering test can return (0, 0). MFENCE or a locked instruction prevents it.
- ARMv8 allows all four reorderings for independent addresses; use dependencies, DMB, or LDAR/STLR to impose order. Publishing data through a flag, as in the MP test, can work on x86 and fail on ARM.
- In C/C++, data races are undefined behaviour. Race-free code using mutexes and seq_cst operations, without weaker synchronisation, has the DRF-SC guarantee. A correct release/acquire protocol can publish data; acquire/release alone does not exclude SB.

## Further reading
- [x86-TSO: a rigorous and usable programmer's model (Sewell et al., CACM)](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~pes20/weakmemory/cacm.pdf)
- [Weak vs strong memory models — Preshing on Programming](https://preshing.com/20120930/weak-vs-strong-memory-models/)
- [Memory reordering caught in the act — Preshing on Programming](https://preshing.com/20120515/memory-reordering-caught-in-the-act/)
- [std::memory_order — cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic/memory_order)
- [Linux kernel memory barriers documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/memory-barriers.txt)

- [Armv8 multicopy-atomic model](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~pes20/armv8-mca/armv8-mca-draft.pdf)

- [C++ draft: data races](https://eel.is/c++draft/intro.races)

- [C++ draft: atomic ordering](https://eel.is/c++draft/atomics.order)

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a multicore system to be **sequentially consistent**?

options.text: Every core sees every write instantly, with zero latency
options.explanation: SC is about ordering, not speed. Writes may take time; what matters is that the result matches some single interleaving.

options.text: The result of any execution matches some single interleaving of all cores' operations, with each core's operations in program order
options.explanation: Correct. This is Lamport's definition: one global sequence, respecting each thread's program order.

options.text: All writes to the same address are seen in the same order by every core
options.explanation: That is cache coherence, which is per-address. SC is a stronger, cross-address guarantee.

options.text: Threads execute one at a time, never in parallel
options.explanation: SC allows true parallel execution. It only requires the outcome to be explainable by some interleaving.

questions.workedExample:
Sequential consistency has two parts:

1. There is **one global order** of all memory operations from all cores.
2. Each core's operations appear in that order **in program order**.

Coherence is the weaker per-address version of point 1. The difference shows up only when a thread reads and writes *different* addresses, as in the store-buffering and message-passing litmus tests.

questions.prompt: For aligned, same-size ordinary accesses to distinct addresses in coherent write-back memory under x86-TSO, which reordering can be observable?

options.text: A later load completing before an earlier store (store → load)
options.explanation: Correct. The per-core store buffer lets a load proceed while an older store is still waiting to become visible. This is the only relaxation in x86-TSO.

options.text: A later store becoming visible before an earlier store (store → store)
options.explanation: x86 drains its store buffer in FIFO order, so stores become visible in program order.

options.text: A later load completing before an earlier load (load → load)
options.explanation: x86 does not let loads appear reordered with older loads. ARM does.

options.text: All four kinds, just like ARM
options.explanation: x86 is much stronger than ARM. It allows only store → load reordering.

questions.workedExample:
Picture x86-TSO as SC plus a FIFO store buffer per core:

- Stores enter the buffer in order and leave in order: no store → store reordering.
- Loads execute in order relative to each other: no load → load.
- A store after a load waits behind it: no load → store.
- But a load can read memory while an older store is still buffered: **store → load is visible**.

questions.prompt: How can a store buffer improve performance by allowing work to continue while a store awaits ownership or visibility?

options.text: To save memory by storing values in compressed form
options.explanation: Store buffers hold pending writes, not compressed data. Their purpose is latency hiding.

options.text: Because cache coherence protocols cannot handle stores at all without it
options.explanation: Coherence protocols handle stores fine; the buffer is there so the core need not *wait* for them.

options.text: It can hold pending stores while independent instructions continue, until capacity or other dependencies limit progress
options.explanation: Correct. The benefit depends on the workload and implementation; it is not necessarily a win on every workload.

options.text: To let programs undo stores after an exception
options.explanation: Speculative state is handled by the reorder buffer; once a store reaches the store buffer as committed it is not undone.

questions.workedExample: A store may wait for a cache line or ownership. Buffering can let independent instructions continue while that wait is unresolved, subject to buffer capacity and other constraints. In the x86-TSO abstraction, later loads to other addresses may observe memory before the store drains, enabling SB outcomes. A buffer need not imply that every implementation exposes weak ordering.

questions.prompt:
Two threads run this x86 assembly-level code, with `x` and `y` initially 0. Assume aligned, same-size ordinary accesses to distinct coherent write-back memory locations, with no other writers or fences. Which final values of (r1, r2) are permitted by x86-TSO? Select all that apply.

```
Thread 1      Thread 2
x = 1         y = 1
r1 = y        r2 = x
```

options.explanation: Possible. Thread 1 runs completely before Thread 2: Thread 1 reads y = 0, then Thread 2 reads x = 1.
Possible. The mirror image: Thread 2 runs first.
Possible. Both stores happen, then both loads, in an interleaving.
Possible on x86. Each store sits in its core's store buffer while the following load reads the old value from memory. SC forbids this; TSO allows it.

questions.workedExample:
Enumerate:

| Outcome | How |
|---|---|
| (0, 1) | T1 entirely first |
| (1, 0) | T2 entirely first |
| (1, 1) | stores, then loads |
| (0, 0) | both stores buffered |

The first three are SC interleavings. (0, 0) needs each load to overtake its own thread's earlier store, which x86's store buffer permits. Adding `mfence` between the store and load in each thread rules (0, 0) out.

questions.prompt: Assume a single machine-level publication using aligned, same-size accesses to distinct initially-zero coherent write-back memory (Arm Normal-memory) locations, with no other writers, barriers or dependencies. A producer writes `data = 42` then `flag = 1` with plain stores; a consumer reads `flag`, then `data`, with plain loads (assume the compiler emits them exactly in this order). The consumer sees `flag == 1`. On which hardware might it still read `data == 0`?

options.text: Neither x86 nor ARM: once the flag is visible, so is the data
options.explanation: This holds on x86 but not on ARM, where the stores or the loads may be reordered.

options.text: Both x86 and ARM
options.explanation: x86 keeps stores in order with stores and loads in order with loads, so message passing works there.

options.text: x86 only, because of its store buffer
options.explanation: The x86 store buffer only allows store → load reordering, which is not what this pattern needs.

options.text: ARM only, because it may reorder the two stores or the two loads
options.explanation: Correct. ARM's weak model allows store → store and load → load reordering for independent addresses, either of which breaks this pattern.

questions.workedExample:
Message passing needs two orderings:

1. The producer's `data` store must be visible before its `flag` store (store → store).
2. The consumer's `flag` load must happen before its `data` load (load → load).

x86 guarantees both. ARMv8 guarantees neither for unrelated addresses. Fix: a release store of the flag (STLR) and an acquire load of it (LDAR), or C11 `memory_order_release` / `memory_order_acquire`, whose compiler mapping must provide the required ordering; exact instructions depend on target and compiler.

questions.prompt: A C++ one-shot producer/consumer publication uses a plain bool ready initially false. Exactly one producer initialises an item, then sets ready; one consumer waits, then reads the item, with no concurrent reuse. The flag is accessed without synchronisation. Which change fixes this publication protocol?

options.text: Mark `ready` as `volatile`
options.explanation: `volatile` in C++ gives neither atomicity nor inter-thread ordering. It would not prevent the reordering.

options.text: Make `ready` a `std::atomic<bool>`, store it with `memory_order_release`, and load it with `memory_order_acquire`
options.explanation: Correct. Release/acquire guarantees that writes before the store are visible to a thread whose acquire load sees it. It also removes the data race (UB).

options.text: Add `sleep(1)` after initialising each item
options.explanation: Timing does not create ordering; it only makes the bug rarer and the service slower.

options.text: Compile with `-O0` so the compiler does not reorder anything
options.explanation: Even without compiler reordering, the ARM hardware can reorder the accesses. Also the code still contains a data race.

questions.workedExample: The unsynchronised flag is a data race on every C++ target, including x86. Under the stated one-shot ownership/lifetime assumptions, an atomic release store and an acquire load that reads it publish the initialised item. Reusable queues need additional ownership, reclamation and reuse protocols. Exact generated instructions and performance depend on compiler and target.

questions.prompt: For a naturally aligned lock-free 32-bit atomic in ordinary write-back memory, suppose the selected x86-64 GCC build compiles a `memory_order_release` atomic store to a plain `mov`, but a `memory_order_seq_cst` store to `xchg`. Why does the seq_cst store need the more expensive instruction?

options.text: A plain `mov` is not atomic on x86
options.explanation: The ordinary aligned32-bit MOV in this question can provide atomic access; its cross-address ordering is the missing issue. Larger, misaligned or special-memory accesses need their own guarantees.

options.text: `xchg` flushes the cache so other cores see the write
options.explanation: `xchg` does not flush caches; coherence handles visibility. It acts as a full barrier.

options.text: seq_cst must forbid the store being reordered with a later seq_cst load, which TSO allows; `xchg` is implicitly locked and acts as a full barrier
options.explanation: Correct. TSO already gives release ordering without an extra hardware instruction for the scoped ordinary accesses, but not store → load ordering. The locked `xchg` drains the store buffer.

options.text: Release stores are not ordered at all on x86
options.explanation: x86 stores are already ordered after earlier loads and stores, which is exactly release semantics, so a plain `mov` suffices.

questions.workedExample:
Compare what each ordering needs with what TSO gives:

- Release: earlier loads and stores may never move after the store. TSO already guarantees this, so `mov` works.
- Seq_cst: additionally, all seq_cst operations form one total order. A seq_cst store followed by a seq_cst load may never be reordered, but TSO allows store → load reordering.

So the compiler uses a locked instruction (`xchg`, or `mov` plus `mfence`), which waits for the store buffer to drain.

questions.prompt: Which statements about C and C++ concurrency are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A data race on a non-atomic variable is undefined behaviour
options.explanation: Correct. The C11 and C++11 memory models make races on non-atomics UB, so the compiler may assume they do not happen.

options.text: `volatile` makes a variable safe to share between threads
options.explanation: False. `volatile` prevents some compiler optimisations, but gives no atomicity and no ordering between threads.

options.text: A data-race-free program using only seq_cst atomics behaves as if sequentially consistent
options.explanation: Correct. This is the DRF-SC guarantee.

options.text: Relaxed atomic fetch_add is suitable for an independent statistics counter when no publication or ordering of other data is required
options.explanation: Correct for the stated purpose. The read-modify-write prevents lost increments; relaxed ordering retains per-object coherence without publishing unrelated data. Reading a live counter is not a synchronised snapshot of other state.

options.text: Testing on x86 is enough to find ordering bugs that would show up on ARM
options.explanation: False. x86 is stronger, so many bugs that weak ordering exposes never manifest there.

questions.workedExample: The true choices are: a C/C++ data race is undefined behaviour; correctly synchronised code using mutexes and seq_cst operations without weaker synchronisation has the DRF-SC guarantee; and relaxed atomic fetch_add can maintain an independent counter. C/C++ volatile does not supply inter-thread synchronisation, and successful tests on x86 do not prove a program correct on every target.

questions.prompt: You implement Peterson's lock for two threads on x86, using aligned ordinary stores and loads to coherent write-back memory in assembly; flag and turn locations are initially set appropriately and there are exactly two participants. Each thread does `flag[me] = 1; turn = other;` and then spins while `flag[other] == 1 && turn == other`. Occasionally both threads enter the critical section. Which listed change is sufficient on both threads before their spin loops?

options.text: Insert `MFENCE` after the stores and before the spin loop's loads
options.explanation: Correct. The failure is store → load reordering: each thread reads the other's flag before its own flag store is visible. A full fence prevents that.

options.text: Insert `SFENCE` between the two stores
options.explanation: SFENCE orders stores with stores, which x86 already does for normal stores. The problem is a load overtaking a store.

options.text: Make the spin loop read `flag[other]` twice
options.explanation: Re-reading does not stop the first read happening before your own store is visible to the other core.

options.text: Nothing can fix it; Peterson's algorithm is incorrect
options.explanation: The algorithm is correct under sequential consistency. It just needs a fence to get SC behaviour on TSO hardware.

questions.workedExample:
Peterson's lock is a store-buffering pattern:

```
T0: flag[0]=1; turn=1
    read flag[1]
T1: flag[1]=1; turn=0
    read flag[0]
```

1. Both threads' stores sit in their store buffers.
2. Each reads the other's flag from memory and sees 0.
3. Both conclude the other does not want the lock, and both enter.

The missing ordering is store → load, the one relaxation TSO has. `MFENCE` (or a locked instruction, or seq_cst atomics in C11) restores it.

questions.prompt:
In the store-buffering test, a developer makes both stores `memory_order_release` and both loads `memory_order_acquire`. Is the outcome `r1 == 0 && r2 == 0` still allowed by the C++ memory model?

```
T1: x.store(1, rel)
    r1 = y.load(acq)
T2: y.store(1, rel)
    r2 = x.load(acq)
```

options.text: No: acquire and release together act as a full fence
options.explanation: Release and acquire are one-way barriers. Together they do not stop a store moving after a later load.

options.text: No, but only on x86
options.explanation: The C++ model permits it independent of the target; ordinary MOV-based x86 mappings also permit it, without guaranteeing that every run observes it.

options.text: Yes. Both acquire loads may read the initial zeros, so no release/acquire synchronises-with edge connects the threads
options.explanation: Correct at the language level. A particular compiler/target may impose stronger ordering and never exhibit it. Using seq_cst on all four operations is sufficient, but not the only possible repair.

options.text: Yes, but only because the variables are not atomic
options.explanation: They are atomics here. The outcome is permitted by the orderings chosen, not by a data race.

questions.workedExample: Assume both atomics initially zero. If both acquire loads read those initial values, neither reads the other thread’s release store, so publication synchronisation does not connect the threads. The language permits (0, 0). Ordinary MOV-based x86 mappings also permit it; some AArch64 mappings can be stronger. Four seq_cst operations prohibit it; properly designed fences or locking are other options.

questions.prompt: In a hardware-level IRIW test, two writers independently set x and y from 0 to 1. Each reader’s two loads are ordered by the specified model: R1 reads x then y, R2 reads y then x. Which model statement about R1 seeing (1, 0) and R2 seeing (1, 0) is correct? Assume ordinary aligned coherent memory and no other writers.

options.text: Yes, on x86, because of the store buffer
options.explanation: x86-TSO gives a global store order and orders these reads; the store buffer does not permit this IRIW outcome.

options.text: A non-multicopy-atomic model may allow it; an appropriately ordered multicopy-atomic model such as x86-TSO forbids it
options.explanation: Correct. With ordered reads, inconsistent propagation to different observers can allow the outcome in a weaker non-MCA model. The revised Armv8-A MCA model also forbids ordered IRIW.

options.text: Yes, on every architecture, because coherence is per-address
options.explanation: Coherence alone would allow it, but x86 and ARMv8 provide multi-copy atomicity, which forbids it.

options.text: No, on every architecture
options.explanation: A suitable non-MCA model can allow the outcome; architecture and barrier choices must be specified before applying the example to hardware.

questions.workedExample: In the forbidden MCA outcome, R1 would require x’s write before y’s write, while R2 would require y’s write before x’s write. With both reader orders preserved, no single globally consistent propagation order satisfies both. A non-MCA model can instead let different observers receive the writes in different orders. C++ acquire-only source code must be analysed at the language level rather than assumed to force an identical hardware mapping everywhere.

questions.prompt: A simple lock implementation releases an aligned lock word with an ordinary store to coherent write-back memory on x86, with compiler ordering preserved. Why can that store provide release ordering?

options.text: x86 stores are always sequentially consistent
options.explanation: TSO permits the store-buffering outcome across stores and later independent loads. Release ordering needs less than a full SC protocol.

options.text: Unlock only needs release semantics, so no earlier access from the critical section moves after it, and TSO already guarantees that for every ordinary store
options.explanation: Correct. TSO forbids load → store and store → store reordering, which is precisely release ordering.

options.text: The x86 cache coherence protocol orders all accesses
options.explanation: Coherence orders writes to one address; it does not order the critical section's accesses (to other addresses) relative to the unlock.

options.text: Unlocking needs no ordering at all
options.explanation: Without release ordering, writes in the critical section could become visible after the lock appears free, letting the next owner see stale data.

questions.workedExample: Under the stated x86-TSO model, earlier stores and loads are ordered before the unlock store. A subsequent successful acquire of the lock can then synchronise with that release under the complete protocol. This is an ordering guarantee, not a claim that every access has reached DRAM. Compiler ordering, correct acquisition, memory attributes and lock ownership still matter; the behaviour is not supplied by cache coherence alone.

lessons.title: SIMD and vectorisation
lessons.summary: How one instruction can process 4, 8 or 16 values at once with SSE, AVX and NEON, what stops compilers vectorising your loops, and how to write code they can.
lessons.body:
Adding two arrays of a million floats takes a million additions. A scalar core does them one per instruction. But the adder hardware is cheap compared with the cost of fetching, decoding and scheduling an instruction. So CPU designers asked: why not make one instruction do *several* additions?

That is **SIMD** (single instruction, multiple data). Each register becomes a wide **vector register** holding several values side by side, called **SIMD lanes**, and one instruction operates on all lanes at once.

```
256-bit AVX register: 8 x float32
ymm1  | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
ymm2  |10 |20 |30 |40 |50 |60 |70 |80 |
       ------ vaddps ymm0,ymm1,ymm2 ----
ymm0  |11 |22 |33 |44 |55 |66 |77 |88 |
```

One instruction, eight results. The possible speedup depends on instruction throughput, dependencies and memory traffic; lane count alone is not a measured speedup.

## The instruction set families

| ISA | Example vector width | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| SSE / SSE2 | 128 bits | x86 packed operations |
| AVX / AVX2 | 256 bits | AVX2 adds many 256-bit integer operations |
| AVX-512 | Up to 512 bits | Feature subsets differ; also supports masking |
| NEON / Advanced SIMD | 128 bits | Arm implementations that support this extension |
| SVE / SVE2 | 128–2048 bits | A power of two (128, 256, 512, 1024 or 2048); early specifications allowed any multiple of 128. Target support required |

How many lanes you get depends on how wide the register is and how wide each element is:

```formula
L = W_reg / W_elem
L = 256 bits / 32 bits = 8
where
L: the number of lanes: how many elements one vector register holds side by side
W_reg: the width of the vector register, in bits; 128, 256 or 512 on x86
W_elem: the width of one element, in bits: 32 for float32, 64 for float64, 8 for int8
bits: binary digits, the unit of register and element width
In words: a register holds as many elements as fit in its width, so a 256-bit AVX register holds eight 32-bit floats.
```

The full table:

| Width | float32 | float64 | int8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 4 | 2 | 16 |
| 256 | 8 | 4 | 32 |
| 512 | 16 | 8 | 64 |

**FMA** (fused multiply-add) is one instruction that multiplies two numbers and adds a third, rounding only once at the end:

```formula
d = a × b + c
where
d: the result written to each lane
a: the first number being multiplied
b: the second number being multiplied
c: the number added to the product
In words: multiply two values and add a third in one step, with a single rounding instead of one after the multiply and another after the add.
```

Counting the multiply and the add as two FLOPs (floating-point operations) can double the arithmetic rate *if* FMA has the same lane count and sustained issue rate as the compared add-only instructions.

Some other notable details:
- **AVX-512** provides eight mask registers (`k0`–`k7`); ordinary EVEX writemasking uses `k1`–`k7`, with a zero mask-field encoding meaning no writemask. Masked operations can help with loop tails and conditionals.
- **SVE** permits vector-length-agnostic programs: correctly written code can adapt to different supported vector lengths without recompilation. Merely using SVE does not make every algorithm independent of vector length.

### Peak throughput

A chip's theoretical peak arithmetic rate multiplies four things together: how many cores it has, how fast each clock ticks, how many vector instructions each core can start per cycle, and how much arithmetic each of those instructions does:

```formula
F_cyc = N_u × L × F_op
F_peak = N_c × f_clk × F_cyc
where
F_cyc: floating-point operations (FLOPs) one core can complete per clock cycle
N_u: the number of vector arithmetic units in a core that can each start an instruction every cycle
L: the number of lanes per vector instruction
F_op: FLOPs per lane per instruction: 2 for an FMA (a multiply and an add), 1 for a plain add or multiply
F_peak: the peak rate of the whole chip, in FLOPs per second (FLOP/s)
N_c: the number of CPU cores
f_clk: the sustained clock frequency, in hertz (Hz), that is cycles per second
In words: peak FLOP rate is cores times cycles per second times the FLOPs each core can do per cycle, and that last figure is units times lanes times FLOPs per instruction.
```

A hypothetical single core sustaining two 256-bit float32 FMAs per cycle at 3 GHz:

```formula
F_cyc = 2 × 8 × 2 = 32
F_peak = 1 × 3 × 10^9 Hz × 32 FLOP
F_peak = 96 × 10^9 FLOP/s = 96 GFLOP/s
where
F_cyc: FLOPs per cycle per core: 2 FMA units × 8 float32 lanes × 2 FLOPs per FMA
F_peak: the peak rate, in FLOPs per second
Hz: hertz, one cycle per second; 3 GHz is 3 × 10^9 Hz
FLOP: one floating-point operation
FLOP/s: floating-point operations per second
GFLOP/s: gigaFLOPs per second, 10^9 FLOP/s
In words: 32 FLOPs per cycle at 3 billion cycles a second is 96 billion FLOPs a second.
```

A hypothetical scalar baseline sustaining one add per cycle delivers 3 GFLOP/s; this compares different operations and assumes the stated throughput. Real peak and useful performance require target-specific instruction and memory measurements.

## Writing SIMD by hand: intrinsics

Compilers expose vector instructions as **intrinsics**, C functions that map almost one-to-one onto instructions. Here is an AVX array addition:

```c
#include <immintrin.h>
#include <stddef.h>

void add(float *a, const float *b,
         const float *c, size_t n) {
  size_t i = 0;
  for (; n - i >= 8; i += 8) {
    __m256 vb = _mm256_loadu_ps(b + i);
    __m256 vc = _mm256_loadu_ps(c + i);
    __m256 va = _mm256_add_ps(vb, vc);
    _mm256_storeu_ps(a + i, va);
  }
  for (; i < n; i++)   /* scalar tail */
    a[i] = b[i] + c[i];
}
```

Precondition: each pointer provides at least n valid floats; the output range does not overlap either input range. The two read-only input ranges may overlap. Compile for an AVX-capable execution environment. These explicit intrinsics do not insert a scalar fallback for unsafe overlap.

Note the two loops. The main loop handles eight elements per iteration; the **tail loop** handles whatever is left over when n is not a multiple of 8:

```formula
N_vec = ⌊n / 8⌋
N_tail = n mod 8
N_vec = ⌊1003 / 8⌋ = 125
N_tail = 1003 mod 8 = 3
where
n: the number of array elements; 1003 in the example
N_vec: the number of main-loop iterations, each handling 8 elements
N_tail: the number of elements the scalar tail loop handles, from 0 to 7
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
mod: the remainder after whole-number division (1003 = 125 × 8 + 3)
8: the lane count of a 256-bit AVX register holding 32-bit floats
In words: 1,003 floats need 125 full eight-lane iterations, and the tail loop finishes the last 3 one at a time.
```

`loadu` means "unaligned load"; its performance depends on the target, alignment, cache-line and page boundaries.

The NEON version looks the same with different names: `float32x4_t`, `vld1q_f32`, `vaddq_f32`, `vst1q_f32`, four lanes at a time.

## Letting the compiler do it: auto-vectorisation

Intrinsics target particular extensions. Auto-vectorisation lets a compiler select transformations for its target and cost model. Current Clang enables loop vectorisation at `-O2`; GCC also enables it at `-O2`, with a more conservative cost model than `-O3`. Check the actual compiler version and optimisation report. On x86, `-mavx2` enables AVX2 instructions; `-march=native` targets the build machine and may produce binaries unsuitable for other machines.

Ask the compiler what it did: `-fopt-info-vec-missed` (GCC) or `-Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize` (Clang).

### What blocks vectorisation

**1. Possible aliasing.** In a scalar array-add loop, if `a` overlaps `b` shifted by one element, one iteration may feed the next. A compiler needs a safe transformation, potentially using a runtime overlap check. The manual compute kernel above instead requires disjoint output. C's `restrict` can express exclusive access to modified objects through the relevant pointer; two read-only inputs may still alias:

```c
void add(float *restrict a,
         const float *restrict b,
         const float *restrict c,
         size_t n);
```

**2. Loop-carried dependencies.** Here each iteration needs the previous result, so lanes cannot run independently:

```c
for (i = 1; i < n; i++)
  a[i] = a[i - 1] * 0.5f + b[i];
```

**3. Floating-point reductions.** Independent partial sums change the addition order. The error can be much larger than a last-bit difference, and overflow or special values can behave differently. Reassociation requires an appropriate numerical contract; GCC's `-fassociative-math` has additional prerequisites, and `-ffast-math` relaxes several rules, not just ordering. Some targets support ordered vector reductions without reassociation. Unsigned integer addition is associative modulo its width; signed overflow is undefined in C. Legal vectorisation still depends on the target and cost model.

**4. Branches.** SIMD lanes cannot take different paths. The compiler may **if-convert** safe work into per-lane selects or masked operations. It cannot blindly evaluate both sides if that introduces invalid accesses, exceptions or observable side effects.

```c
/* compare/select candidate */
for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
  a[i] = b[i] > 0 ? b[i] : 0;
```

Simple conditionals vectorise well. Complicated ones, or ones calling functions, usually do not.

**5. Non-contiguous memory.** Contiguous access is convenient for vector loads. Strided or indexed access may use scalar loads, wider loads with shuffles, or **gather instructions** when supported. Relative cost depends on the target, addresses and cache behaviour.

### Data layout: structure of arrays

That last point makes layout matter. An **array of structures** interleaves fields:

```
AoS: x y z x y z x y z x y z
SoA: x x x x | y y y y | z z z z
```

To update all `x` coordinates, AoS needs strided access; **structure of arrays** gives contiguous vectors. Game engines, physics codes and columnar databases use SoA for this reason.

## SIMD in the real world

Numeric libraries can combine compiled loops, CPU dispatch and SIMD. NumPy supports baseline and dispatch compute kernels selected for supported CPU features; use of a SIMD path depends on the operation, dtype, layout, build and runtime environment. Avoiding Python interpreter overhead is a separate benefit.

```python
import numpy as np
a = np.ones(1_000_000, dtype=np.float32)
b = np.ones(1_000_000, dtype=np.float32)
c = a + b  # SIMD path depends on build
```

## Pitfalls and trade-offs

- **Bandwidth ceiling.** Once the relevant bandwidth is saturated, faster arithmetic alone cannot remove that traffic limit. SIMD may still help reach the ceiling by changing instruction overhead or memory concurrency. Roofline is an upper bound, not proof of the actual bottleneck.
- **Portability.** Unsupported vector instructions can fault. Runtime dispatch must check CPU features *and* operating-system support for the required register state; for AVX this includes appropriate OSXSAVE/XGETBV checks. Use a supported dispatcher rather than testing one CPUID bit. Keep baseline code free of instructions unsupported on the baseline.
- **Frequency and power.** Sustained clock and vector throughput depend on the processor and workload; measure the selected target.
- **Floating-point results.** Reassociation or contraction into FMA can change results. Validate error tolerances and special-value behaviour before enabling transformations. Vectorisation itself need not reorder a reduction.
- **Short loops.** Setup, checks and tails can outweigh the gain; the threshold is workload-dependent.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> A product-by-product SIMD release history, generic speedup ranges and claims about which vector length most products use is omitted because reliable coverage of those hardware and benchmark specifics was not established in this review.

## Key takeaways
- SIMD makes one instruction work on several lanes: 4 floats in 128-bit SSE or NEON, 8 in AVX, 16 in AVX-512.
- Two 8-lane FMAs issued each cycle give a theoretical 32 FLOPs per cycle; ISA support alone does not promise that throughput.
- Compilers auto-vectorise simple loops; aliasing, loop-carried dependencies, FP reduction semantics, complex branches and scattered memory can constrain them.
- Use `restrict`, structure-of-arrays layout and vectoriser reports to help the compiler; reach for intrinsics only for hot kernels.
- SIMD speeds up compute-bound loops; memory-bound loops are limited by bandwidth instead.
