questions.prompt: How many 32-bit floats fit in one 256-bit AVX `ymm` register?

options.explanation: That is a 128-bit SSE or NEON register: 128 / 32 = 4.
That is a 512-bit AVX-512 register: 512 / 32 = 16.
32 is the number of 8-bit integers in a 256-bit register, not 32-bit floats.
Correct. 256 bits / 32 bits per float = 8 lanes.

questions.workedExample:
The lane count is the register width divided by the element width:

```formula
L = W_reg / W_elem
L = 256 bits / 32 bits = 8
where
L: the number of lanes: elements held side by side in one register
W_reg: the register width, in bits; 256 for a ymm register
W_elem: the element width, in bits; 32 for a float32
bits: binary digits
In words: eight 32-bit floats fill a 256-bit register.
```

The same register holds 256 / 64 = 4 float64 values or 256 / 8 = 32 int8 values. So one `vaddps` on `ymm` registers performs 8 single-precision additions.

questions.prompt: A vectorised loop over n array elements processes 8 elements per iteration. The compiler also emits a second, scalar loop after it. What is that second loop for?

options.text: To check the vector results are correct
options.explanation: Compilers do not double-check arithmetic; the scalar loop does different work.

options.text: To handle the leftover elements when n is not a multiple of 8
options.explanation: Correct. This is the tail loop, also called a remainder loop or epilogue loop. With n = 1003 it runs 3 times.

options.text: To process elements whose addresses are unaligned
options.explanation: Modern unaligned vector loads handle misalignment; the tail is about the count, not alignment.

options.text: It is dead code left over from optimisation
options.explanation: It is essential: without it, the last few elements (the remainder when n is divided by 8) would never be computed.

questions.workedExample:
The vector loop runs while at least 8 elements remain:

```c
/* vector: 8 at a time */
for (; n - i >= 8; i += 8) ...
/* tail: leftovers */
for (; i < n; i++) ...
```

The tail mops up the remainder:

```formula
N_tail = n mod 8
N_tail = 1003 mod 8 = 3
where
N_tail: the number of elements the scalar tail loop handles, 0 to 7
n: the number of array elements; 1003 in the example
mod: the remainder after whole-number division (1003 = 125 × 8 + 3)
In words: whatever does not fill a final group of eight is left to the tail loop.
```

AVX-512 mask registers and ARM SVE predicates let compilers instead run one final masked vector iteration with only some lanes switched on.

questions.prompt: Why can FMA double a hypothetical CPU's peak FLOP rate when it has the same lane count and sustained instruction rate as the compared add-only implementation?

options.text: It runs at twice the clock speed of other instructions
options.explanation: FMA runs at the normal clock. The gain comes from doing more work per instruction.

options.text: It uses twice as many lanes
options.explanation: FMA uses the same register widths as other vector instructions.

options.text: It computes a × b + c in one instruction, which counts as two floating-point operations, at the same throughput as a plain add or multiply
options.explanation: Correct. Same instruction rate, two FLOPs each, so twice the peak FLOPs.

options.text: It avoids rounding, so results need no correction step
options.explanation: FMA does round only once, which helps accuracy, but that is not why the FLOP count doubles.

questions.workedExample:
Peak FLOPs per cycle multiply the number of units, the lanes per instruction and the FLOPs each lane does:

```formula
F_cyc = N_u × L × F_op
F_add = 2 × 8 × 1 = 16
F_fma = 2 × 8 × 2 = 32
where
F_cyc: floating-point operations (FLOPs) per clock cycle
N_u: vector units that can each start an instruction every cycle; 2 here
L: lanes per instruction; 8 float32 lanes in 256 bits
F_op: FLOPs per lane per instruction: 1 for an add, 2 for an FMA (multiply and add)
F_add: FLOPs per cycle using adds only
F_fma: FLOPs per cycle using FMAs
In words: the same instruction rate with twice the work per instruction doubles the peak.
```

Matrix multiply and dot products are naturally multiply-then-add, so they can use FMA for almost every operation.

questions.prompt: A 4-core server CPU runs at 2.5 GHz. Each core sustains two 512-bit float32 FMAs per cycle at that clock. What is its theoretical peak single-precision throughput?

options.text: 640 GFLOP/s
options.explanation: Correct. 2 units × 16 lanes × 2 FLOPs = 64 FLOPs per cycle per core; × 4 cores × 2.5 × 10⁹ = 640 × 10⁹.

options.text: 320 GFLOP/s
options.explanation: This forgets that each FMA counts as two FLOPs.

options.text: 160 GFLOP/s
options.explanation: This uses only one FMA unit and counts each FMA as one FLOP.

options.text: 1,280 GFLOP/s
options.explanation: This double-counts something: 512-bit registers hold 16 floats, not 32.

questions.workedExample:
Build it up from one lane to the whole chip:

```formula
L = 512 / 32 = 16
F_cyc = N_u × L × F_op
F_cyc = 2 × 16 × 2 = 64
F_peak = N_c × f_clk × F_cyc
F_peak = 4 × 2.5 × 10^9 Hz × 64
F_peak = 640 × 10^9 FLOP/s
where
L: float32 lanes in a 512-bit register
F_cyc: FLOPs per cycle per core
N_u: FMA units per core; 2
F_op: FLOPs per FMA lane; 2 (multiply and add)
F_peak: the chip's peak, in FLOPs per second
N_c: the number of cores; 4
f_clk: the clock frequency, in hertz (Hz); 2.5 GHz = 2.5 × 10^9 Hz
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
FLOP/s: floating-point operations per second; 640 × 10^9 FLOP/s = 640 GFLOP/s
In words: 64 FLOPs per cycle per core, times 4 cores, times 2.5 billion cycles a second, is 640 GFLOP/s.
```

This is an arithmetic ceiling. Approaching it requires enough independent FMAs and data supply while sustaining the stated clock; other instructions may issue concurrently.

questions.prompt: Which loops permit the indicated direct lane-wise transformation, assuming valid disjoint output ranges, read-only inputs, supported operations and no reassociation of floating-point sums? For reductions, consider independent partial sums combined at the end. This is a legality question, not a promise that a compiler chooses vectorisation. Select all that apply.

options.text: `for (i=0;i<n;i++) a[i] = b[i] * c[i];` (floats)
options.explanation: Eligible: each multiplication is independent; the same per-element operation can be performed in lanes.

options.text: `for (i=1;i<n;i++) a[i] = a[i-1] + b[i];` (floats)
options.explanation: Not vectorised directly. Each iteration needs the previous result, a loop-carried dependency.

options.text: `for (i=0;i<n;i++) s += x[i];` with uint32_t elements and uint32_t s
options.explanation: Eligible: addition modulo 2^32 is associative, so partial sums preserve the final uint32_t value.

options.text: `for (i=0;i<n;i++) s += x[i];` with `float` elements
options.explanation: Independent partial sums change the floating-point order and are not permitted by this question. Ordered vector reductions are a different transformation.

options.text: `for (i=0;i<n;i++) a[i] = b[i] > 0 ? b[i] : 0;` (floats)
options.explanation: Eligible with a compare/select that preserves the scalar floating-point semantics, including NaN and signed-zero behaviour.

questions.workedExample: Independent products and safe per-element compare/selects can run in lanes. Unsigned 32-bit sums can use partial sums because modulo addition is associative. The recurrence needs earlier results, and independent float partial sums change rounding order. Thus options 1, 3 and 5 satisfy the stated transformation rules. Actual compiler selection still depends on target support and profitability.

questions.prompt: A compiler rejects a proposed transformation of a sequential float sum into several independent partial sums, with strict floating-point ordering required. Why?

options.text: Floats cannot be stored in vector registers
options.explanation: SSE and AVX registers hold floats perfectly well; `addps` adds four of them.

options.text: Independent partial sums reorder the additions; floating-point addition is not associative, so the result could change
options.explanation: Correct. This transformation changes the arithmetic order. Ordered vector reductions can preserve the order on targets that support them.

options.text: The loop has unknown trip count `n`
options.explanation: Unknown trip counts are routine; the compiler adds a tail loop.

options.text: The variable `total` might alias `x`
options.explanation: `total` is a local scalar whose address is not taken, so the compiler knows it cannot alias the array.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the orders:

```formula
s_seq = ((x[0] + x[1]) + x[2]) + …
P_k = x[k] + x[k + 8] + x[k + 16] + …
s_vec = Σ P_k   for k = 0 to 7
where
s_seq: the scalar sum, added strictly left to right
x: the array being summed; x[0] is its first element
P_k: the partial sum kept in lane k
k: the lane number, 0 to 7
s_vec: the vectorised sum: the eight partial sums added at the end
Σ: sum of: add up the terms for every listed value of k
…: and so on, to the end of the array
In words: the vector version adds the same numbers in a different order, eight interleaved running totals combined at the end.
```

Mathematically identical, but each floating-point addition rounds, so a different order can give a substantially different result. A tiny example: (1e20 + −1e20) + 1 = 1, but 1e20 + (−1e20 + 1) = 0 in float32. Any reassociation must be allowed by the numerical contract.

options.text: Change `int i` to `long i`
options.explanation: The index type is not the problem the compiler reported.

options.text: Add `-ffast-math`
options.explanation: Fast-math relaxes floating-point rules; it does not tell the compiler the pointers do not overlap.

options.text: Mark the pointers `restrict` to promise `a` and `b` do not overlap
options.explanation: Correct. If `a` might point one element after `b`, iteration i's store could feed iteration i + 1's load. `restrict` rules that out.

options.text: Unroll the loop by hand four times
options.explanation: Unrolling does not resolve the aliasing question and may make the loop harder to analyse.

questions.workedExample:
Why aliasing matters:

1. Suppose `a == b + 1`.
2. Then `a[i] = b[i] * 2` writes `b[i+1]`.
3. Iteration i + 1 must read that new value. Loading 8 of b at once would read stale values.

With `float *restrict a, float *restrict b` you promise no overlap, so vectorising is safe. (Compilers sometimes emit a runtime overlap check instead, but the promise must be true for every call; adding it to an overlapping call introduces undefined behaviour.)

questions.prompt: An AVX2 loop handles 8 floats per vector iteration followed by a scalar tail loop. For n = 1003, how many times does each loop body run?

options.text: 126 vector iterations, 0 tail iterations
options.explanation: 126 × 8 = 1008 would run past the end of the array.

options.text: 125 vector iterations, 3 tail iterations
124 vector iterations, 11 tail iterations
options.explanation: The vector loop continues while at least 8 elements remain, so it would take another 8 from those 11.

options.text: 1003 vector iterations, 0 tail iterations
options.explanation: That is the scalar loop's count; vector iterations each cover 8 elements.

questions.workedExample:
Divide with remainder:

```formula
N_vec = ⌊n / 8⌋ = ⌊1003 / 8⌋ = 125
N_tail = n mod 8 = 1003 mod 8 = 3
125 × 8 + 3 = 1003
where
n: the number of elements; 1003
N_vec: the number of vector iterations, 8 elements each
N_tail: the number of scalar tail iterations
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
mod: the remainder after whole-number division
In words: 125 full groups of eight cover 1,000 elements, and the tail does the last 3.
```

With `for (; n - i >= 8; i += 8)`, the last vector iteration starts at `i = 992` (992 + 8 = 1000, which is at most 1003). Then `i = 1000`, and 1008 is more than 1003, so the tail handles 1000, 1001, 1002.

questions.prompt: For disjoint cold arrays of 100 million float32 values, an AVX2 array-add compute kernel is only 1.1× faster than the scalar version. Measurements show both runs nearly saturate sustained DRAM bandwidth and neither has a substantial frequency drop. What best explains the small gain?

options.text: Memory bandwidth limits the loop: each element requires two input loads and an output store, potentially plus write-allocation traffic
options.explanation: Correct under the measured conditions. Faster arithmetic cannot remove the saturated traffic requirement.

options.text: AVX2 has no instruction for float addition
options.explanation: `vaddps` on `ymm` registers is AVX (and available with AVX2); float addition is fully supported.

options.text: The CPU must be downclocking heavily under AVX2
options.explanation: The stated measurements rule out a substantial clock reduction in these runs; no universal downclock limit is assumed.

options.text: Unaligned loads are always 8× slower
options.explanation: There is no universal eightfold penalty; alignment and boundary-crossing costs are target-dependent.

questions.workedExample:
Count bytes, then divide by bandwidth:

```formula
D = 10^8 × 16 B = 1.6 × 10^9 B
t_min = D / R
t_min = 1.6 × 10^9 B / (50 × 10^9 B/s)
t_min = 0.032 s = 32 ms
P_max = 10^8 FLOP / 0.032 s
P_max ≈ 3.125 × 10^9 FLOP/s
where
D: total DRAM traffic, in bytes (B): 100 million elements × 16 bytes each (4 + 4 read, 4 read-for-ownership, 4 written back)
t_min: the shortest possible run time at full bandwidth, in seconds (s)
R: the sustained bandwidth; a hypothetical 50 GB/s = 50 × 10^9 B/s
P_max: the highest useful addition rate this traffic allows
B: byte
s: second
ms: millisecond, 0.001 s
FLOP: one floating-point operation (one addition here)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: moving 1.6 GB at 50 GB/s takes at least 32 ms whatever the arithmetic does, which caps the loop at about 3 billion additions a second.
```

Useful traffic is only 12 bytes per element; the extra 4 is the write-allocate read. This is a traffic bound, not proof that an arbitrary scalar loop reaches it; the prompt supplies the bandwidth measurements. Non-temporal stores or existing cached output can change the model.

options.text: Build for a baseline such as x86-64 (SSE2) and add runtime dispatch, so hot functions are also compiled for AVX2 and selected after checking all required CPU and OS register-state features
options.explanation: Correct. A supported multiversioning or dispatch mechanism can select a compatible compute kernel while the rest of the binary retains its baseline requirements.

options.text: Use `-march=native` on your build machine

options.text: Switch to AVX-512, which is backwards compatible

Dispatch only after checking every required extension and OS-enabled register state; AVX requires more than its CPUID feature bit. Test both fallback and accelerated paths. Feature-level names and -march targets may include instructions beyond AVX2 alone.

Assume 4-byte floats, a 24-byte struct with no padding, unchanged arithmetic order and contraction rules, and large valid disjoint arrays. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: With SoA, eight consecutive `x` values sit next to each other, so one contiguous vector load fetches them
options.explanation: Correct. Each field becomes its own dense array, matching how SIMD lanes are loaded.

options.text: With AoS, consecutive `x` values are 24 bytes apart, so vectorising needs strided or gather loads, or shuffles
options.explanation: Correct under the stated layout: the stride is 24 bytes. A compiler may use gathers or loads and shuffles; relative performance is target-dependent.

options.text: SoA also uses each cache line more fully for this loop, since no bytes are wasted on y, z, vy, vz
options.explanation: Correct for a long sweep: only two of six float fields are needed. Edge lines and alignment affect exact line utilisation.

Across a long sweep only 8 of every 24 data bytes are useful to this loop; exact line edges vary. SoA is not universally best, and layout alone does not change results when arithmetic and contraction are preserved. The correct choices are the first three.

questions.prompt: Profiling shows 70% of a program's time is in a loop. You vectorise it with AVX and the loop itself runs exactly 8× faster. Assume the remaining work and all overhead are unchanged. What is the overall speedup?

options.explanation: Only the loop speeds up; the other 30% of the time is unchanged.
This multiplies 0.7 by 8, which is not how speedups combine.

options.text: About 2.6×
About 3.3×
options.explanation: That is the limit 1 / 0.3 if the loop took zero time, not the 8× case.

questions.workedExample:
Amdahl's law applies to any partial speedup:

```formula
S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f / k)
S = 1 / (0.3 + 0.7 / 8)
S = 1 / (0.3 + 0.0875) = 1 / 0.3875
S ≈ 2.58
where
S: the overall speedup of the program
f: the fraction of time in the vectorised loop; 0.7
k: how many times faster the loop becomes; 8
≈: approximately equal to
In words: an 8× faster loop that is 70% of the time makes the whole program only about 2.6× faster.
```

Even infinite vector width would only give 1 / 0.3 ≈ 3.3×. To go further, look at the remaining 30%.

lessons.title: GPU architecture: SIMT, warps and memory
lessons.summary: How a GPU runs tens of thousands of threads by grouping them into warps, why branch divergence and uncoalesced memory access hurt, and how the GPU memory hierarchy shapes fast kernels.
lessons.body:
CPUs and GPUs make different trade-offs among latency, throughput, control and data movement. This lesson describes CUDA on NVIDIA GPUs, focusing on exposing enough independent work to keep execution units busy. The sketch is conceptual, not a transistor-area measurement.

```
CPU core              GPU SM
+----------------+    +----------------+
| control | big  |    |ALU ALU ALU ALU |
| logic   | cache|    |ALU ALU ALU ALU |
|---------+------|    |ALU ALU ALU ALU |
| ALU  ALU  ALU  |    |ALU ALU ALU ALU |
+----------------+    | small cache    |
 latency-optimised    +----------------+
                       throughput-optimised
```

NVIDIA groups execution resources into **streaming multiprocessors** (SMs). SM counts, execution throughput, cache sizes and memory bandwidth vary by product and configuration. A marketing “core” count is not directly comparable with a CPU core count.

## The programming model

In CUDA you write a **GPU kernel**: a function that describes what *one* thread does. You then launch it over a **CUDA grid** of **CUDA blocks** (thread blocks).

```cpp
#include <stddef.h>

__global__ void saxpy(size_t n, float a,
                      const float *x,
                      float *y) {
  size_t i = (size_t)blockIdx.x * blockDim.x
           + threadIdx.x;
  if (i < n)            /* guard tail */
    y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i];
}

/* 256 threads per block */
size_t blocks = n / 256 + (n % 256 != 0);
if (n != 0) {
  /* require blocks <= device grid limit */
  saxpy<<<(unsigned)blocks, 256>>>(
      n, 2.0f, dx, dy);
}
```

- Each thread computes a global index from its block and thread indices, and handles one element (the formulas follow this list).
- A **thread block** executes on a single SM. Its size must satisfy device and GPU kernel limits. Threads can use block shared memory and a correctly participating block-wide `__syncthreads()` barrier.
- Ordinary blocks must be schedulable independently and may run in any order. Explicit cooperative and thread-block-cluster facilities add separate synchronisation contracts.
- `dx` and `dy` must designate at least n GPU-accessible floats. The output must never overlap input at a shifted index; otherwise threads can race. Unified or mapped memory can also be GPU-accessible. This launch fragment assumes allocated, initialised storage, a checked grid limit and a supported 256-thread block. Production code must check launch errors and completion before consuming results.

The index each thread computes places the blocks one after another along the array:

```formula
i = b × N_b + t
i = 3 × 256 + 10 = 778
where
i: the thread's global index: which array element it handles
b: the block's index within the grid, counting from 0 (blockIdx.x in CUDA); here 3
N_b: the number of threads per block (blockDim.x); here 256
t: the thread's index within its own block, from 0 to N_b − 1 (threadIdx.x); here 10
In words: skip over all the earlier blocks, each N_b threads long, then count along to your own position in your block.
```

The launch needs enough blocks to cover every element, so the block count is rounded up. The code's `n / 256 + (n % 256 != 0)` is integer division plus one extra block when there is a remainder:

```formula
N_blocks = ⌈n / N_b⌉
N_blocks = ⌈1,000 / 256⌉ = ⌈3.9⌉ = 4
where
N_blocks: the number of blocks launched
n: the number of array elements; 1,000 in the example
N_b: the number of threads per block; 256
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up to the next whole number
In words: launch enough blocks that blocks times threads per block is at least the element count; the surplus threads (here 4 × 256 − 1,000 = 24) fail the i < n guard and do nothing.
```

## Warps and SIMT

CUDA forms each block’s threads into **GPU warps** of 32 consecutive linear thread indices. A warp instruction is issued to an active subset of its logical threads; a partially filled warp has fewer active participants. Thirty-two logical threads do not imply 32 dedicated physical ALUs or one-cycle execution of every instruction.

NVIDIA calls this **SIMT** (single instruction, multiple threads). You write per-thread code while hardware tracks thread state and participation. Independent thread scheduling means implicit lockstep is not a valid synchronisation contract.

### Branch divergence

What happens when threads in one warp disagree at a branch?

```cpp
if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0)
  a();   /* even threads */
else
  b();   /* odd threads */
```

In a simplified masked-execution model, the warp issues the a-path instructions for even lanes and the b-path instructions for odd lanes. Each path uses half the logical lanes. The functions here stand for arbitrary branch bodies; actual scheduling, predication and elapsed cost depend on the code and target.

```
time ->   a() a() a()  b() b() b()
even ln   ### ### ###  ... ... ...
odd ln    ... ... ...  ### ### ###
```

A warp-uniform condition can avoid within-warp path divergence when that transformation preserves the algorithm. Branching on `threadIdx.x / 32 % 2` illustrates this for a one-dimensional block; it does not make all branch overhead disappear.

Since Volta, **independent thread scheduling** tracks per-thread execution state. It can make older implicit warp-synchronous code **unsafe**. Communicating threads must use the appropriate synchronisation primitive, such as `__syncwarp(mask)`, and obey its participant-mask and memory-ordering rules. It is not enough to assume that two threads belong to the same warp.

## Hiding latency with many warps

Long-latency memory operations need not stall every resident warp. The SM retains execution state for several warps and can issue work from a ready warp while another waits. This avoids an operating-system context switch; it does not make scheduling physically free or guarantee that every cycle has an issuable instruction. Resident-warp limits and issue resources depend on the target.

```
cycle:  1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8
warp 0  ld .  .  .  .  .  .  add
warp 1  .  ld .  .  .  .  .  .
warp 2  .  .  mul mul ld .  .  .
warp 3  .  .  .  .  .  mul mul .
```

How many memory requests must be outstanding to keep the memory system busy? **Little's law**, a result from queueing theory that holds for any system in steady state, answers it: the average amount in the system equals the rate it flows through times the average time each piece spends inside.

```formula
D = R × t_res
D = 10^12 B/s × 400 × 10^-9 s
D = 4 × 10^5 B = 400 KB
where
D: the average number of bytes in flight: requested but not yet delivered, in bytes (B)
R: the byte throughput, in bytes per second (B/s); 1 TB/s = 10^12 B/s in the example
t_res: the average residence time: how long each request is outstanding, in seconds (s); 400 ns = 400 × 10^-9 s
B: byte, 8 bits
s: second
KB: kilobyte, 1,000 bytes
In words: to stream 1 TB/s when each request takes 400 ns to come back, about 400 KB of requests must be in flight at any moment.
```

The law needs a steady state and a consistent definition of bytes and time. More resident warps can expose additional independent requests, but do not guarantee them.

### Occupancy

**GPU occupancy** is the number of warps resident on an SM divided by the most it can hold. Registers are one limit: every resident thread needs its own registers from the SM's register file, so the more registers each thread uses, the fewer threads fit. In a hypothetical SM with 65,536 32-bit registers and a 64-warp limit, 64 registers per thread give:

```formula
O = W_res / W_max
N_t = R_SM / r
N_t = 65,536 / 64 = 1,024
W_res = N_t / 32 = 1,024 / 32 = 32
O = 32 / 64 = 0.5
where
O: occupancy, from 0 to 1 (0.5 is 50%)
W_res: the number of warps resident on the SM at once
W_max: the most warps the SM can hold; 64 here
N_t: the most threads the register file can hold
R_SM: the number of 32-bit registers in the SM's register file; 65,536 here
r: the registers each thread of the GPU kernel uses; 64 here
32: the number of threads in a warp
In words: 64 registers per thread let only 1,024 threads, or 32 warps, fit in the register file, which is half of the SM's 64-warp limit.
```

Occupancy is limited by whichever resource runs out first:

- **Registers**, as above. Allocation granularity, thread-block size and other limits can lower occupancy; 32 registers per thread does not guarantee 100%.
- **GPU shared memory.** With 164 KiB actually available for blocks and 48 KiB allocated per block, shared capacity permits at most three blocks, before other constraints (worked below).
- **Thread-block size and limits.** Resident-block limits and the placement of whole blocks can bind before register or thread limits.

```formula
N_blk = ⌊M_SM / M_blk⌋
N_blk = ⌊164 KiB / 48 KiB⌋ = ⌊3.4⌋ = 3
where
N_blk: the most blocks that fit by shared-memory capacity
M_SM: the GPU shared memory available for blocks on the SM, in kibibytes (KiB); 164 KiB here
M_blk: the GPU shared memory each block allocates, in KiB; 48 KiB here
KiB: kibibyte, 1,024 bytes
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number, because a block cannot be partly resident
In words: three 48 KiB blocks use 144 KiB; a fourth would need 192 KiB, more than the 164 KiB available.
```

Higher occupancy can help hide latency when it exposes more useful independent work. It is not worth maximising for its own sake: additional registers or GPU shared memory per thread may improve reuse enough to outweigh fewer resident warps.

## The memory hierarchy

| Storage | Typical CUDA visibility |
|---|---|
| Registers | Per-thread values; spills may use memory |
| GPU shared memory | Block-local, with explicit cluster extensions |
| L1 / L2 caches | Hardware-managed; scope and policy depend on target |
| Global memory | Addressable across the grid under memory-ordering rules |

On supported architectures, thread-block clusters provide **distributed shared memory**, allowing access to another block’s GPU shared memory within the cluster. Correct cluster synchronisation and storage lifetimes are required; ordinary non-cluster blocks do not get that access.

### Coalescing

For the 32-byte-sector coalescing model used here, assume 32 active threads, one 4-byte load each, a 32-byte-aligned base and a first global index that is a multiple of 32. Consecutive x[i] accesses touch four sectors. These are requested sectors, not necessarily DRAM transfers: caches can satisfy requests. Misalignment can increase the count.

| Pattern | Sectors per warp |
|---|---|
| `x[i]` | 4 |
| `x[2 * i]` | 8 |
| `x[32 * i]` | 32 |
| random | up to 32 |

With a stride of 32, each thread's float lands in its own sector. Utilisation compares the bytes the threads wanted with the bytes in the sectors fetched:

```formula
U = N_use / N_sec
N_use = 32 × 4 B = 128 B
N_sec = 32 × 32 B = 1,024 B
U = 128 B / 1,024 B = 0.125
where
U: sector utilisation: the fraction of requested sector bytes the warp actually uses (0.125 is 12.5%)
N_use: useful bytes: 32 threads × one 4-byte float each
N_sec: requested sector bytes: 32 sectors × 32 bytes each
B: byte, 8 bits
In words: each thread wants 4 bytes but drags in a whole 32-byte sector, so only one byte in eight is useful.
```

That is why GPU code prefers structure-of-arrays layouts and why you transpose data on the way into GPU shared memory.

### GPU shared memory and bank conflicts

GPU shared memory is a programmer-managed scratchpad; its latency advantage depends on the target, access pattern and compared cache/memory path. A classic pattern is **tiling**: each block loads a tile of a matrix into GPU shared memory once, then every thread reuses it many times.

In the bank model here, successive 4-byte words map across 32 **shared-memory banks**. If the 32 threads of a warp hit 32 different banks, the access takes one pass. If several threads hit *different addresses in the same bank*, the request needs multiple bank-service passes; same-word reads can instead broadcast. These are logical passes, not a universal cycle count. Reading a column of a `float tile[32][32]` has every thread in the same bank: a 32-way conflict. Padding the row to 33 floats (`tile[32][33]`) shifts each row by one bank and removes it. The bank arithmetic shows why:

```formula
m = (a / 4) mod 32
m_32 = (32 × r + c) mod 32 = c
m_33 = (33 × r + c) mod 32
m_33 = (r + c) mod 32
where
m: the bank holding the 4-byte word at byte address a, from 0 to 31
a: the byte address of the word within GPU shared memory; the tile is assumed to start at address 0 (bank 0), so element [r][c] of a 32-float-row tile is word 32 × r + c
4: each bank is 4 bytes wide, so a / 4 is the word number
32: the number of banks
mod: the remainder after whole-number division (40 mod 32 = 8)
r: the row of the tile element; in a column read, thread r of the warp reads row r
c: the column being read, the same for every thread
m_32: the bank of element [r][c] when each row holds 32 floats
m_33: the bank of element [r][c] when each row is padded to 33 floats
In words: with 32-float rows every element of a column lands in the same bank, c; with 33-float rows each row moves one bank along, so the 32 threads hit 32 different banks.
```

## Real-world use and trade-offs

- **Matrix units.** Supported GPUs provide specialised matrix operations with specific shape, dtype and numerical contracts. Their operation counts are not directly comparable with arbitrary scalar arithmetic workloads.
- **Data transfer.** Include transfers, synchronisation and launch overhead in the end-to-end timing. Keeping data resident across GPU kernels can amortise movement; asynchronous overlap needs suitable hardware, buffers and dependencies.
- **Launch overhead.** Tiny GPU kernels can be dominated by launch and scheduling costs. Fusion or CUDA Graphs may help, but should be measured.
- **Access patterns.** Serial pointer chains, divergent work and scattered addresses can limit GPU performance. Algorithm and layout transformations may change that outcome.
- **Precision.** Check the selected device and operation’s supported precision, accuracy and throughput; no generic FP64-to-FP32 ratio applies to all GPUs.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> A complete A100/H100 and AMD configuration catalogue, generic launch/latency timings and universal throughput ratios is omitted because those version- and workload-specific values were not comprehensively verified here; the retained arithmetic examples state their hypothetical assumptions.

## Key takeaways
- GPUs expose substantial throughput through parallel work; execution and memory resources depend on the target.
- GPU kernels are written per thread and launched as a grid of blocks; each block runs on one SM and uses that SM's GPU shared memory.
- CUDA warps contain 32 logical threads. Instructions run on active subsets; use explicit synchronisation rather than assuming lockstep.
- Latency is hidden by switching between many resident warps; occupancy is limited by registers, GPU shared memory and block limits.
- Make warps read contiguous memory (coalescing), avoid shared-memory bank conflicts, and keep data on the GPU to avoid PCIe transfers.

questions.prompt: On NVIDIA GPUs, what is a **GPU warp**?

options.text: A group of 32 logical threads whose instructions are issued to active subsets under the SIMT execution model
options.explanation: Correct. Divergence, partial warps and independent thread scheduling mean not every logical thread must execute each issued instruction.

options.text: Another name for a thread block
options.explanation: A block can contain up to 1,024 threads, i.e. many warps. The block is the unit of scheduling onto an SM; the warp is the unit of instruction issue.

options.text: A single CUDA core
options.explanation: A CUDA core is one FP32 arithmetic unit. A warp is a group of threads, not a piece of hardware.

options.text: The full set of blocks launched by a GPU kernel
options.explanation: That is the grid.

questions.workedExample:
The hierarchy, from big to small:

```
grid   all blocks of one launch
block  <= 1024 threads, one SM
warp   32 threads; active subsets
thread one index, own registers
```

The thread-block size you choose is split into warps: 256 threads per block makes 8 warps. Choosing a thread-block size that is not a multiple of 32 wastes lanes in the last warp.

questions.prompt: How can an SM issue useful work while one resident warp waits for a long-latency memory operation?

options.text: It predicts every load address in advance and prefetches perfectly
options.explanation: GPUs do have caches and some prefetching, but they do not rely on perfect prediction.

options.text: It runs at a much higher clock than a CPU
options.explanation: A higher clock is not the mechanism described; readiness-based issue can overlap work at a given clock.

options.text: It retains several warps and can issue from a ready warp while another waits
options.explanation: Correct. Resident state avoids an OS context switch, and independent work may overlap the wait. Scheduling and instruction-issue limits still apply.

options.text: It stalls, but has so many cores that it does not matter
options.explanation: If every warp simply stalled, the cores would sit idle. The point is that there are enough *other* ready warps.

questions.workedExample: In a hypothetical SM with 48 resident warps, warp 0 issues a load and waits. A scheduler may issue a ready instruction from another warp. Hiding the delay requires enough independent issuable work and available execution resources; merely launching many threads does not guarantee full utilisation.

questions.prompt: In a GPU kernel launched with `blockDim.x = 256`, what global index `i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x` does thread 10 of block 3 compute?

options.explanation: This adds 256 + 10, treating block 3 as if it were block 1.
This multiplies the thread index by the threads-per-block count, which is backwards.
This adds the block and thread indices without scaling by the threads-per-block count.

questions.workedExample:
Blocks are laid out one after another:

```
block 0: i = 0   .. 255
block 1: i = 256 .. 511
block 2: i = 512 .. 767
block 3: i = 768 .. 1023
```

So thread 10 of block 3 is:

```formula
i = b × N_b + t
i = 3 × 256 + 10 = 768 + 10 = 778
where
i: the global index
b: the block index (blockIdx.x); 3
N_b: threads per block (blockDim.x); 256
t: the thread index within the block (threadIdx.x); 10
In words: skip three whole blocks of 256 threads, then count 10 more.
```

The answer is **778**. Local threads 0 to 31 of that block have global indices 768 to 799 and form one warp, and they read consecutive elements, so the access is coalesced.

questions.prompt: In one warp, threads with even `threadIdx.x` take an `if` branch costing 100 cycles and odd threads take the `else` branch costing 60 cycles. Assume the simplified model runs the masked paths consecutively, with no overlap and negligible additional control overhead. Roughly how long does the warp spend on this `if/else`?

options.text: 100 cycles, the longer of the two
options.explanation: That would be true if the two paths ran in parallel, but a warp executes one instruction stream at a time.

options.text: 80 cycles, the average
options.explanation: Each lane does wait for both paths; averaging does not describe the warp's time.

options.text: 60 cycles
options.explanation: The `if` path alone takes 100 cycles.

options.text: About 160 cycles: both paths run one after the other with lanes masked
options.explanation: Correct. Divergence runs the paths one after the other. Each runs at 50% lane utilisation.

questions.workedExample:
Step through what the warp does:

1. Evaluate the condition per lane: mask = even lanes.
2. Run the `if` body (100 cycles) with odd lanes masked off.
3. Invert the mask and run the `else` body (60 cycles).
4. Reconverge.

```formula
t_warp ≈ t_if + t_else
t_warp ≈ 100 + 60 = 160
where
t_warp: the time the warp spends on the if/else, in clock cycles
t_if: the time of the if path; 100 cycles
t_else: the time of the else path; 60 cycles
≈: approximately equal to (control overhead ignored)
In words: a divergent warp runs both paths one after the other, so their times add.
```

Total ≈ **160 cycles**. If the condition were uniform per warp, for example `(threadIdx.x / 32) % 2`, each warp would take only its own path: 100 or 60 cycles.

questions.prompt: An SM has 65,536 32-bit registers and supports at most 64 resident warps (2,048 threads). Your GPU kernel uses 128 registers per thread. Ignoring block/allocation granularity and all other limits, what is the maximum occupancy?

options.explanation: At 128 registers per thread, 2,048 threads would need 262,144 registers, four times what the SM has.
50% corresponds to 64 registers per thread.
This halves the figure again; 512 threads fit, not 256.

questions.workedExample:
Compute how many threads the register file can hold, then convert to warps:

```formula
N_t = R_SM / r = 65,536 / 128 = 512
W_res = N_t / 32 = 512 / 32 = 16
O = W_res / W_max = 16 / 64 = 0.25
where
N_t: the most threads the register file can hold
R_SM: 32-bit registers in the SM; 65,536
r: registers per thread; 128
W_res: resident warps (32 threads each)
O: occupancy (0.25 is 25%)
W_max: the SM's warp limit; 64
In words: 128 registers per thread leave room for only 16 of the 64 possible warps.
```

Is 25% bad? For a memory-bound GPU kernel it may be, because fewer warps means less latency hiding. For a compute-bound GPU kernel that uses those registers to keep tiles in fast storage, it can be optimal. Measure rather than chase 100%.

questions.prompt: Each thread in a warp reads one 4-byte float from `x[4 * i]`, where i is the global thread index. The memory system moves data in 32-byte sectors. Assume 32 active threads, a 32-byte-aligned base and a first i that is a multiple of 32. What fraction of the requested sector bytes is used by this instruction?

options.explanation: Only fully contiguous access (stride 1) uses every byte. Stride 4 skips three of every four floats.
Correct. Addresses from byte 0 through byte 499 touch 16 aligned sectors covering 512 bytes, of which 128 are useful.
That would be stride 8. With stride 4, each 32-byte sector contains two useful floats.
Even stride 32 has one 4-byte word per 32-byte sector, giving 12.5%, not 3%.

questions.workedExample:
Thread k reads the float at byte offset 16 × k (4 floats × 4 bytes), so the threads touch offsets 0, 16, 32, …, 496. The last float ends at byte 499, so sixteen aligned 32-byte sectors cover the accesses.

```formula
N_use = 32 × 4 B = 128 B
N_sec = 16 × 32 B = 512 B
U = N_use / N_sec = 128 / 512 = 0.25
where
N_use: useful bytes: 32 threads × one 4-byte float
N_sec: bytes in the requested sectors
U: utilisation (0.25 is 25%)
B: byte
In words: each 32-byte sector holds two of the wanted floats, so a quarter of the fetched bytes are used.
```

Cache hits and reuse can change actual DRAM traffic. Layout or cooperative loading may improve utilisation, but loading extra unwanted fields alone does not eliminate their transfer cost.

questions.prompt: For ordinary CUDA blocks without thread-block clusters or cooperative cross-block facilities, which statements are true? Use linear thread indices and correctly participating barriers. Select all that apply.

options.text: All threads of a block run on the same SM
options.explanation: Correct. This is why they can share the SM's GPU shared memory.

options.text: Threads in the same block can synchronise with `__syncthreads()`
options.explanation: Correct. It is a barrier for all threads of one block.

options.text: Blocks of the same grid can be relied on to run in a fixed order
options.explanation: False. Blocks may run in any order, concurrently or one after another; correct code must never depend on order.

options.text: Threads in different blocks can read each other's GPU shared memory
options.explanation: False in this scope. Cluster distributed shared memory is a separate supported facility with explicit synchronisation and lifetime requirements.

options.text: A block's threads are divided into warps of 32 consecutive threads
options.explanation: Correct. Threads 0–31 form warp 0, 32–63 warp 1, and so on.

questions.workedExample: Correct choices: a block executes on one SM; its participating threads can use a block-wide barrier; consecutive linear IDs form warps. Ordinary blocks have no fixed execution order and cannot directly read each other’s block-local GPU shared memory. Thread-block clusters extend the latter rule under an additional API contract.

questions.prompt: You launch `saxpy` for 1,000,000 elements (`n`) with 256 threads per block, using `blocks = (n + 255) / 256`. How many blocks are launched, and why does the GPU kernel need `if (i < n)`?

options.text: 3,906 blocks; the guard is only for safety and never triggers
options.explanation: 3,906 × 256 = 999,936, which leaves 64 elements unprocessed. Integer division rounds down; the + 255 rounds up.

options.text: 3,907 blocks; the last block has 3,907 × 256 − 1,000,000 = 192 surplus threads that must never write out of bounds
options.explanation: Correct. Rounding up guarantees coverage; the guard stops the extra threads touching memory past the end.

options.text: 1,000,000 blocks, one per element
options.explanation: Each block contains 256 threads, so you need about n / 256 blocks.

options.text: 3,907 blocks; the guard prevents branch divergence
options.explanation: The guard prevents out-of-bounds access. Here n is divisible by 32: the final block has two fully active warps and six fully inactive warps, so this guard does not split a warp.

questions.workedExample:
Calculate:

```formula
N_blk = ⌈n / N_b⌉
N_blk = ⌈1,000,000 / 256⌉
N_blk = ⌈3,906.25⌉ = 3,907
N_x = N_blk × N_b − n
N_x = 1,000,192 − 1,000,000 = 192
where
N_blk: the number of blocks launched
n: the number of elements; 1,000,000
N_b: threads per block; 256
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up to a whole number (what (n + 255) / 256 does in integer arithmetic)
N_x: the surplus threads with no element to process
In words: 3,907 blocks are needed to cover every element, which launches 192 more threads than there are elements.
```

Those 192 threads compute an index at or beyond n. Without the guard they would read and write past the end of the arrays. It is the GPU version of a SIMD tail loop.

questions.prompt: A job processes 4 GB of input and produces 4 GB of output. On the CPU it takes 0.2 s. On the GPU the GPU kernel takes 5 ms, but data starts and ends in host memory and crosses a PCIe link sustaining about 25 GB/s each way, used one direction at a time. Assume transfers and computation do not overlap and omit any further overhead. Is offloading worthwhile?

options.text: Yes: 5 ms is 40× faster than 0.2 s
options.explanation: This ignores the transfers, which dominate here.

options.text: Yes, about 2× faster overall
options.explanation: Do the transfer arithmetic: 8 GB over 25 GB/s alone is 0.32 s.

options.text: It depends only on the GPU's FLOP rate
options.explanation: The measured GPU kernel time is already given. A FLOP ceiling alone would not determine it, and transfer costs must also be counted.

options.text: No: transfers take about 0.32 s, so the GPU path is about 0.325 s versus 0.2 s on the CPU
options.explanation: Correct. Unless the data can stay on the GPU across many operations, or transfers overlap with other work, the CPU wins.

questions.workedExample:
Total GPU time is copy in, plus GPU kernel, plus copy out:

```formula
t_in = 4 GB / (25 GB/s) = 0.16 s
t_out = 4 GB / (25 GB/s) = 0.16 s
t_gpu = t_in + t_k + t_out
t_gpu = 0.16 + 0.005 + 0.16 = 0.325 s
where
t_in: time to copy the input over PCIe, in seconds (s)
t_out: time to copy the output back, in seconds (s)
t_k: the GPU kernel time; 5 ms = 0.005 s
t_gpu: the total GPU path time
GB: gigabyte, 10^9 bytes
GB/s: gigabytes per second
s: second
In words: the copies take 0.32 s, far more than the 0.005 s GPU kernel, so the GPU path is slower than the 0.2 s CPU run.
```

The GPU kernel is 40× faster but only about 1.5% of the GPU path. This is Amdahl's law again. Real systems keep data resident on the GPU (deep-learning frameworks keep weights and activations there), overlap copies with compute using streams, or use faster interconnects.

link.title: CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide — NVIDIA

questions.prompt: A transpose GPU kernel loads a 32 × 32 tile of floats into `__shared__ float tile[32][32]` and then each warp reads a *column*: thread k reads `tile[k][c]`. GPU shared memory has 32 banks, each 4 bytes wide. What happens, and what is the usual fix?

options.text: No problem: GPU shared memory has no access restrictions
options.explanation: GPU shared memory is banked; simultaneous accesses to different addresses in one bank are handled one after another.

options.text: A 32-way bank conflict, because every element in a column lies in the same bank; pad the array to `tile[32][33]`
options.explanation: Correct. Each row is 32 floats = 128 bytes, so column elements are 128 bytes apart and map to the same bank. One float of padding shifts each row by one bank.

options.text: Uncoalesced global memory access; use a larger thread-block size
options.explanation: The tile is already in GPU shared memory; coalescing concerns global memory. The issue here is banks.

options.text: A 2-way bank conflict; use `double` instead of `float`
options.explanation: The conflict is 32-way, and switching to doubles changes the data type rather than fixing the layout.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
m = (a / 4) mod 32
m_32 = (32 × k + c) mod 32 = c
m_33 = (33 × k + c) mod 32
m_33 = (k + c) mod 32
where
m: the bank of the 4-byte word at byte address a, 0 to 31
a: the byte address in GPU shared memory
32: the number of banks
mod: the remainder after whole-number division
k: the row read by thread k of the warp
c: the column being read, the same for all threads
m_32: the bank of tile[k][c] with 32-float rows
m_33: the bank of tile[k][c] with rows padded to 33 floats
In words: with 32-float rows every thread lands in bank c; padding each row by one float moves each row one bank along.
```

Without padding, all 32 accesses hit one bank and are handled one after another in 32 passes. With padding, each thread hits a different bank: one pass. The cost is 32 wasted floats per tile.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical steady-state memory model, throughput is 2 TB/s and average byte residence time is 500 ns. By Little's law, what is the average data in flight? Use decimal units.

options.text: About 1 KB
options.explanation: This is 1,000 times smaller than the product of the given rate and average time.

options.text: About 1 GB
options.explanation: That overestimates by a factor of 1,000; check the units of nanoseconds.

options.text: About 1 MB
options.explanation: Correct. 2 × 10¹² B/s × 500 × 10⁻⁹ s = 10⁶ bytes.

options.text: Little's law does not apply to memory systems
options.explanation: Little's law applies to any queueing system in steady state, including outstanding memory requests.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
D = R × t_res
D = 2 × 10^12 B/s × 500 × 10^-9 s
D = 10^6 B = 1 MB
where
D: average bytes in flight, in bytes (B)
R: throughput; 2 TB/s = 2 × 10^12 B/s
t_res: average residence time; 500 ns = 500 × 10^-9 s
B: byte
s: second
MB: megabyte, 10^6 bytes (decimal)
In words: 2 TB/s with requests outstanding for 500 ns means about 1 MB in flight on average.
```

If a hypothetical 108-SM device shared this load evenly, the average would be about 9,259 bytes per SM, or 72.34 requests of 128 bytes. This is a steady-state average, not a required occupancy at every instant. The GPU kernel needs enough independent requests and resources; high warp occupancy is only one possible contributor.

questions.prompt: Which patterns raise clear GPU-efficiency concerns before workload-specific restructuring and measurement? Treat these as warning signs, not proofs that no GPU implementation can win. Select all that apply.

options.text: Traversing a long linked list where each node's address comes from the previous node
options.explanation: Poor fit. It is serial: each step depends on the last, so there is no parallelism to spread across threads, and the loads cannot be coalesced.

options.text: Multiplying two 8,192 × 8,192 matrices
options.explanation: Regular matrix work exposes substantial parallelism. Use of tensor operations depends on supported shapes and precision, including the required numerical accuracy.

options.text: A tree search where each thread follows a different data-dependent path with many branches
options.explanation: This can cause divergence and scattered loads; reorganising traversal or grouping work may improve it.

options.text: Applying the same colour correction to every pixel of a 4K video
options.explanation: Good fit. Millions of independent, identical operations on contiguous data.

options.text: Running a single small calculation on data in host memory, once
options.explanation: Transfer and launch costs may dominate a small one-off calculation; compare end-to-end timings.

questions.workedExample: The linked-list dependency chain, divergent tree traversal and one-off small host-resident job are the warning signs. Matrix and pixel workloads expose regular parallel work. Actual suitability still depends on layout, precision, batching, data residency and implementation; benchmark equivalent results end to end.

lessons.title: Accelerators: TPUs, FPGAs and ASICs
lessons.summary: How specialised hardware can improve efficiency, how a TPU's systolic array multiplies matrices, what FPGAs are good for, and when offloading is worth it.
lessons.body:
General-purpose execution spends energy on control and data movement as well as arithmetic. An accelerator can improve efficiency by specialising the computation, reusing operands and amortising instruction overhead. The benefit depends on workload, precision, utilisation, memory traffic and implementation; no universal energy ratio applies.

Power and thermal constraints helped motivate specialisation alongside architectural and process improvements. A **hardware accelerator** provides hardware suited to a class of operations, usually working with a host processor.

## Flexibility and specialisation

| Device | Relevant capability |
|---|---|
| CPU | General instruction execution and control |
| GPU | Many parallel threads and specialised execution units |
| FPGA | Configurable logic and routing for custom circuits |
| ASIC | Silicon designed for a particular application or domain |

This is not a universal efficiency ranking. An FPGA can implement a direct hardware pipeline without fetching one instruction per operation, but can also contain hard or soft processors. An ASIC may include programmable processors and configurable accelerators; “application-specific” does not mean every behaviour is permanently fixed.

## TPUs and the systolic array

By 2013 Google estimated that if people used voice search for a few minutes a day, running the neural networks on CPUs would need it to roughly double its data-centre capacity. So it built the **Tensor Processing Unit** (TPU), deployed in 2015 and described in a 2017 paper.

The first TPU was an inference chip built around one thing: a **256 × 256 matrix multiply unit** of 8-bit integer multiply-accumulate cells (MAC cells), 65,536 in all, at 700 MHz. Its peak rate is the number of MAC cells times the operations each does per cycle times the clock rate:

```formula
P_peak = N_MAC × 2 × f_clk
P_peak = 65,536 × 2 × 700 × 10^6 Hz
P_peak ≈ 91.8 × 10^12 ops/s ≈ 92 TOPS
where
P_peak: the peak arithmetic rate, in operations per second (ops/s)
N_MAC: the number of MAC cells: 256 × 256 = 65,536
2: each multiply-accumulate counts as two operations, a multiply and an add
f_clk: the clock frequency, in hertz (Hz); 700 MHz = 700 × 10^6 Hz
Hz: hertz, one cycle per second
ops: operations (here 8-bit integer multiplies and adds)
s: second
TOPS: tera-operations per second, 10^12 ops/s
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 65,536 cells each doing a multiply and an add 700 million times a second give about 92 trillion operations a second, if every cell is busy every cycle.
```

It also had 28 MiB of on-chip SRAM (a 24 MiB unified buffer for activations plus accumulators) and read weights from 8 GiB of DDR3 at about 34 GB/s. For the paper’s six production inference applications and compared Haswell CPU and NVIDIA K80 GPU systems, the authors reported average performance gains of roughly 15–30× and performance-per-watt gains of 30–80×. These are results of that study, not a guarantee for arbitrary networks or modern devices.

### How a systolic array works

The key idea is to reuse data as it moves through a grid of processing elements (PEs), reducing repeated operand movement. An operand read from a local buffer can serve several operations; a large tiled problem may still require repeated DRAM reads. Each PE multiplies, adds, and passes values to its neighbours, like blood pulsed through the body (hence "systolic").

```
       b-col0  b-col1  b-col2
         v       v       v
a-row0> [PE]--> [PE]--> [PE]
         |       |       |
a-row1> [PE]--> [PE]--> [PE]
         |       |       |
a-row2> [PE]--> [PE]--> [PE]
```

In the *output-stationary* variant, PE(i, j) accumulates C[i][j]. Row i of A enters from the left, delayed by i cycles; column j of B enters from the top, delayed by j cycles. So the values meeting at a PE on a given cycle are fixed by the cycle number and the two delays:

```formula
k = t − i − j
C[i][j] ← C[i][j] + A[i][k] × B[k][j]
0 ≤ k ≤ n − 1
where
k: the index of the term being multiplied on this cycle
t: the clock cycle, counting from 0
i: the row of the PE, which is also the row of A and of C it handles
j: the column of the PE, which is also the column of B and of C it handles
A: the left input matrix, entering row by row from the left
B: the right input matrix, entering column by column from the top
C: the output matrix, one element accumulating in each PE
n: the matrix size (all three are n × n)
←: "is updated to": the PE adds the new product to its running total
≤: less than or equal to
In words: on cycle t the PE in row i, column j multiplies the k-th term pair, where k is the cycle number minus both delays, and it works only on cycles where k is a real index from 0 to n − 1.
```

The following ideal output-stationary model assumes one MAC operation per active PE per cycle and square matrices. It is an explanatory schedule, not an implementation of TPU v1’s exact datapath. Python integer inputs give exact integer results; floating-point inputs have Python’s rounding semantics:

```python
def systolic(A, B):
    n = len(A)
    if len(B) != n or any(
        len(row) != n
        for M in (A, B) for row in M
    ):
        raise ValueError("invalid shape")
    C = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    pes = [(i, j) for i in range(n)
           for j in range(n)]
    for t in range(3 * n - 2):  # cycles
        for i, j in pes:
            k = t - i - j
            if 0 <= k < n:
                C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j]
    return C

print(systolic([[1, 2], [3, 4]],
               [[5, 6], [7, 8]]))
# [[19, 22], [43, 50]]
```

How long does one product take, and how busy is the array during it? The bottom-right PE finishes last: its row and column delays are both as large as possible, and it must still work through every term. The array does one useful MAC operation per term per output element, spread over all its PEs:

```formula
t_last = (n − 1) + (n − 1) + (n − 1)
t_tot = t_last + 1 = 3 × n − 2
U = n^3 / (n^2 × (3 × n − 2))
U = n / (3 × n − 2)
U = 2 / (3 × 2 − 2) = 2 / 4 = 0.5
U → 1/3   as n → ∞
where
t_last: the cycle on which the bottom-right PE does its last MAC operation: its row delay (n − 1), plus its column delay (n − 1), plus the last term index (n − 1)
t_tot: the number of cycles one n × n product takes, counting from cycle 0
n: the matrix size; the substitution line uses n = 2
U: the average utilisation: the fraction of PE-cycles that do a useful MAC operation
n^3: the number of MACs the product needs: n^2 output elements, each a sum of n products
n^2: the number of PEs in the array
→: approaches, gets ever closer to
∞: infinity: n grows without limit
In words: a single square product keeps the array only partly busy, because it takes time to fill and drain; for large arrays the average is about one third, not 100%.
```

For n = 2 the work takes 4 cycles: cycle 0 activates only PE(0,0), cycles 1 and 2 have three PEs busy, and cycle 3 only PE(1,1). That is 8 busy PE-cycles out of 16, the 0.5 above. The utilisation **approaches one third**. A longer reduction dimension or an appropriately overlapped stream of tiles can amortise fill and drain costs.

Why this is efficient:

- In the illustrated full n × n output tile, each operand entering from the local buffer is reused n times along a row or column. Edge tiles and other dataflows differ.
- Local neighbour communication reduces repeated operand access. The simple PE does not decode an instruction for each MAC operation, but the full accelerator still needs buffers and control.
- The ideal schedule is regular. Real hardware also handles stalls, tiling, memory transfers and supported numerical modes.

The TPU used a *weight-stationary* variant: weights are preloaded into the PEs, activations flow across, and partial sums flow down.

### Later TPUs

Later TPU generations added floating-point support for training. **bfloat16** stores 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 7 fraction bits, versus float32’s 23 stored fraction bits. Its normal exponent range is similar to float32’s, but precision, largest finite value and subnormal behaviour differ.

On Cloud TPU, XLA’s float32-to-bfloat16 conversion uses round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, overflows to infinity and flushes bfloat16 subnormals to zero. It is **not** simply mantissa truncation. The wider exponent field relative to IEEE binary16 can reduce the need for loss scaling, but overflow, underflow and numerical accuracy remain workload-dependent. Check the selected TPU generation and operation rather than assuming a single matrix-array configuration across all versions.

## FPGAs: rewirable hardware

A **field-programmable gate array** is a grid of configurable logic connected by a programmable routing fabric:

- **LUTs** (look-up tables): a small memory holding one output bit for every combination of its inputs. A 4-input LUT stores 16 bits, so it can represent any Boolean function of those four inputs; available input counts depend on the device (4 to 6 is common).
- **Flip-flops** for state and pipelining.
- **DSP blocks**: hard multiply-accumulate units.
- **Block RAM**: small on-chip memories spread across the chip.

You can describe a circuit in an HDL such as Verilog or VHDL, or use high-level synthesis for supported source programs. Tools synthesise, place and route the design and generate configuration data. Timing closure, verification and limits on chip resources remain hardware-design tasks.

A custom hardware pipeline can process several inputs concurrently at different stages. Its clock, initiation interval and end-to-end latency depend on the design, data width, memory access and backpressure. A one-item-per-cycle pipeline does not automatically accept a complete variable-length packet every cycle or guarantee fixed network latency.

FPGAs are useful for reconfigurable hardware pipelines and prototyping logic before fabricating a chip. Their configurable routing has costs, but performance and economic comparisons require a particular design and deployment volume.

## ASICs: application-specific silicon

An **application-specific integrated circuit** is designed for an application or domain. Development includes design, verification and manufacturing preparation; costs and lead times vary substantially. A custom implementation can remove configurability overhead, but it is not universally the best performance-per-watt choice for every workload.

Fixed gates cannot be rewritten by loading an FPGA bitstream. However, firmware, programmable processors, configuration registers and supported algorithm parameters may let an ASIC adapt to changes within its design. An algorithm change does not automatically make every ASIC obsolete.

## When is offloading worth it?

1. **Amdahl.** Only the offloaded part speeds up. For fixed work with unchanged remaining time and no added overhead, a 50% accelerated fraction has a 2× speedup ceiling.
2. **Data movement.** Copying inputs to the device and results back can exceed the compute saved. Accelerators work best when data stays on the device across many operations.
3. **Batching versus latency.** Some accelerator workloads benefit from batching; others already expose enough parallelism within one request. A single request may wait for a batch to form, raising latency.
4. **Numerics.** Supported precision varies. Quantisation or mixed-precision execution requires validation against the application’s accuracy and special-value requirements.
5. **Software.** An accelerator is only as useful as its compiler and libraries. Compiler and library support, operation coverage and deployment tooling affect usable performance.
6. **Utilisation.** Peak TOPS remains an arithmetic ceiling, but does not predict bandwidth-limited layer performance. The TPU paper found several production networks were limited by memory bandwidth, not MACs, which the roofline model in the next lesson makes precise.

The first two points combine into one estimate. Normalise the original run time to 1, and add the transfer time to Amdahl's formula:

```formula
S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f / k + x)
S = 1 / (0.2 + 0.8 / 10 + 0.1)
S = 1 / 0.38 ≈ 2.6
where
S: the overall speedup of the whole job
f: the fraction of the original run time that is offloaded; here 0.8
k: how many times faster the accelerator runs that part; here 10
x: the time added by copying data to and from the device, as a fraction of the original run time; here 0.1
≈: approximately equal to
In words: offloading 80% of a job to a device that is 10 times faster, at a copying cost of 10% of the original time, makes the whole job only about 2.6 times faster.
```

Even with an infinitely fast accelerator this job could not beat 1 / (0.2 + 0.1) ≈ 3.3×, because the untouched work and the copies remain.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Generic picojoule ratios, FPGA clock/build/financial-market latency ranges, ASIC dollar/lead-time estimates and a cross-generation accelerator catalogue is omitted because comparable primary evidence for those design-specific claims was not reliably established; they are not needed for the retained mechanism and arithmetic examples.

## Key takeaways
- Specialisation can reduce control overhead and data movement; savings must be evaluated for the workload and numerical contract.
- FPGA logic is field-configurable; ASICs target an application but may still contain programmable components.
- TPU v1 had 65,536 int8 MACs at 700 MHz, giving about 92 TOPS when counting a MAC operation as two operations.
- The illustrated single-product output-stationary array is busy only about one third of the time for large arrays, because of fill and drain; reuse alone does not guarantee peak throughput.
- Offloading pays when saved computation exceeds transfer, setup and any other added costs while preserving required results.

questions.prompt: Why can a specialised accelerator do far more arithmetic per joule than a general-purpose CPU core built on the same process?

options.text: Its multipliers and adders use a fundamentally cheaper kind of transistor
options.explanation: A fundamentally different transistor is not required. Specialised arithmetic, control and data movement can improve efficiency within a process.

options.text: It can reduce or amortise instruction-control overhead and data movement for a suitable workload
options.explanation: Correct. Reuse and specialised execution can reduce energy per useful result; the magnitude depends on design, precision and utilisation.

options.text: Accelerators run at much higher clock speeds
options.explanation: Higher clock is not required; TPU v1’s reported clock was 700 MHz. Clock rate alone does not determine energy per result.

options.text: Accelerators do not need memory, so they avoid DRAM entirely
options.explanation: They still need memory; the TPU read weights from DDR3 and later HBM. They reduce how often each value is fetched, but cannot avoid fetching it.

questions.workedExample: A specialised datapath can reuse operands locally and perform a regular sequence with less per-operation instruction control. This can reduce overhead relative to a general-purpose implementation, but does not eliminate storage or control. Compare equivalent precision and useful results across the whole system rather than assuming a universal per-operation energy ratio.

link.title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a TPU (Jouppi et al., 2017)

questions.prompt: Which device provides a field-configurable logic fabric that can implement a direct hardware pipeline without fetching an instruction for each operation?

options.text: A GPU
options.explanation: A GPU fetches and decodes instructions; it just shares each one across a warp of threads.

options.text: An ASIC
options.explanation: A conventional ASIC’s fabricated logic is fixed, though it may include programmable processors or configurable functions. It does not provide the FPGA fabric described.

options.text: An FPGA
options.explanation: Correct. Its LUTs, flip-flops, DSP blocks and routing are configured by a bitstream, so the circuit is the program, and a new bitstream gives a new circuit.

options.text: A CPU with a large instruction cache
options.explanation: A big I-cache makes fetching cheaper but the CPU is still driven by an instruction stream.

questions.workedExample: An FPGA bitstream configures logic and routing for a circuit. That circuit may be a direct hardware pipeline or even a soft processor executing instructions. Reconfigurable fabric is the distinguishing feature; “no instruction stream anywhere” is not a valid definition of all FPGAs or ASICs.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical accelerator has a 128 × 128 array of multiply-accumulate units (MAC units) clocked at 1 GHz. Assume each unit sustains one MAC operation per cycle. Counting each MAC operation as two operations, what is its peak throughput?

options.text: About 16 TOPS
options.explanation: This counts each MAC operation as one operation. A MAC operation is a multiply and an add, so it is two.

options.text: About 256 GOPS
options.explanation: This uses 128 × 2 instead of 128 × 128: it counts one row of the array, not the whole grid.

options.text: About 65 TOPS
options.explanation: This uses a 256 × 256 array (65,536 MACs) counted once per cycle. The array here is 128 × 128.

options.text: About 33 TOPS
options.explanation: Correct. 16,384 MACs × 2 ops × 10⁹ cycles/s ≈ 32.8 × 10¹² ops/s.

questions.workedExample:
Work it out the same way as the TPU v1 figure in the lesson:

```formula
N_MAC = 128 × 128 = 16,384
P_peak = N_MAC × 2 × f_clk
P_peak = 16,384 × 2 × 10^9 Hz
P_peak ≈ 32.8 × 10^12 ops/s ≈ 33 TOPS
where
N_MAC: the number of MAC units in the array
2: each MAC operation counts as two operations, a multiply and an add
f_clk: the clock frequency; 1 GHz = 10^9 Hz
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
P_peak: the peak rate, in operations per second (ops/s)
ops: operations
s: second
TOPS: tera-operations per second, 10^12 ops/s
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 16,384 units each doing two operations a billion times a second give about 33 trillion operations a second.
```

For comparison, TPU v1 was 65,536 MACs × 2 × 700 MHz ≈ 92 TOPS. Peak assumes every MAC unit is busy every cycle, which requires a suitable schedule, enough independent work and adequate data supply; large dimensions alone do not ensure it.

questions.prompt:
Use the lesson's output-stationary systolic array of processing elements (PEs). On each clock cycle, the PE in row i and column j multiplies one pair of terms, chosen by:

```formula
k = t − i − j
C[i][j] ← C[i][j] + A[i][k] × B[k][j]
0 ≤ k ≤ n − 1
where
k: the index of the term pair used on this cycle; the PE is idle when k is outside 0 to n − 1
t: the clock cycle, counting from 0
i: the PE's row
j: the PE's column
A: the left input matrix
B: the right input matrix
C: the output matrix being accumulated
n: the matrix size
←: is updated to
≤: less than or equal to
In words: the term index is the cycle number minus the row and column delays.
```

With n = 4, what does PE(1, 2) compute at cycle 4?

options.explanation: Correct. The term index is 4 − 1 − 2 = 1, so PE(1, 2) multiplies A[1][1] by B[1][2] and adds it to C[1][2].
This uses the cycle number as the term index. Row 1 is delayed by 1 cycle and column 2 by 2 cycles, so you must subtract both delays.

options.text: Nothing; it is idle at cycle 4
options.explanation: It is idle only when the term index falls outside 0 to 3. Here it is 1, which is valid.
This uses the PE's column number as the term index. The term index depends on the cycle and both delays.

questions.workedExample:
1. Row 1 of A enters 1 cycle late; column 2 of B enters 2 cycles late.
2. So the values meeting at PE(1, 2) on cycle 4 have:

```formula
k = t − i − j
k = 4 − 1 − 2 = 1
where
k: the term index
t: the cycle; 4
i: the PE's row; 1
j: the PE's column; 2
In words: on cycle 4, PE(1, 2) works on term 1.
```

3. So the PE computes A[1][1] × B[1][2] and adds it to C[1][2].

PE(1, 2) is active for terms 0 to 3, which is cycles 3 to 6. The whole 4 × 4 multiply finishes after 3 × 4 − 2 = 10 cycles (cycles 0 to 9), with PE(3, 3) doing its last MAC operation on cycle 9.

questions.prompt: What is a numerical advantage of bfloat16 over IEEE binary16 for some training workloads?

options.text: bfloat16 has more mantissa bits, so it is more precise than FP16
options.explanation: bfloat16 has 7 stored fraction bits versus binary16’s 10, so it has less significand precision.

options.text: Its 8-bit exponent gives a much wider normal exponent range than binary16 while using half the storage of float32
options.explanation: Correct. This can reduce range-related difficulties, but accuracy and underflow still need testing. Cloud TPU conversion rounds to nearest, ties to even, and flushes bfloat16 subnormals; it is not simple truncation.

options.text: bfloat16 is an integer format, so it needs no floating-point hardware
options.explanation: bfloat16 is a floating-point format: sign, exponent and mantissa. Integer formats like int8 were what TPU v1 used for inference.

options.text: bfloat16 uses 8 bits, so twice as many values fit in memory as FP16
options.explanation: bfloat16 is 16 bits, the same size as FP16. It splits those bits differently.

questions.workedExample: Stored sign/exponent/fraction bits are float32: 1/8/23, binary16: 1/5/10, and bfloat16: 1/8/7. Binary16’s largest finite value is 65,504. Bfloat16 has a wider normal exponent range but lower precision than binary16. Some training workflows benefit from loss scaling; the need depends on numerical behaviour. Accumulation precision and conversion rules must be checked for the actual operation.

questions.prompt: A job spends 60% of its time on matrix multiplies. Moving them to an accelerator makes them 20× faster, but copying data to and from the device adds time equal to 10% of the original runtime. Assume unchanged remaining work and no overlap or other overhead. What is the overall speed-up?

options.text: About 20×
options.explanation: Only 60% of the work gets the 20× speed-up. The other 40% and the transfer time do not shrink.

options.text: About 2.3×
options.explanation: This is Amdahl's law without the transfer cost: 1 / (0.4 + 0.03) ≈ 2.33. The copies add another 0.1.

options.text: About 1.9×
options.explanation: Correct. New time = 0.4 + 0.6/20 + 0.1 = 0.53 of the original, so the speed-up is 1 / 0.53 ≈ 1.89×.

options.text: About 1.1×
options.explanation: A speedup of 1.1× would require total time about 0.9091, hence transfer overhead about 0.4791 of the original runtime with the same compute times.

questions.workedExample:
Normalise the original runtime to 1.

```formula
T_new = (1 − f) + f / k + x
T_new = 0.40 + 0.6 / 20 + 0.10
T_new = 0.40 + 0.03 + 0.10 = 0.53
S = 1 / T_new = 1 / 0.53 ≈ 1.89
where
T_new: the new run time, as a fraction of the original
f: the fraction offloaded; 0.6
k: the accelerator's speed-up on that part; 20
x: the transfer time, as a fraction of the original; 0.10
S: the overall speed-up
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the untouched 40% and the 10% of copying leave the job at 53% of its old time, a speed-up of about 1.9×.
```

With the fixed 0.10 transfer cost, the infinite-compute-speed limit is 1/(0.4 + 0.1) = 2×. If transfers were eliminated, it would be 2.5×. Data residency can amortise transfers across operations; it does not automatically eliminate every transfer.
